extraction.body: From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance , the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines. The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves. These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand. So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean. While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it? Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions. This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers. Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam" . Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets. In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes. In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump. Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto. Brit says he is not elusive Bitcoin creator named by New York Times Seven wild moments from the turbulent story of Bitcoin Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name. Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes. The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy , external used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain. A crypto exchange is the digital platform where investors can buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies. Similar to traditional investing, a crypto exchange acts as a brokerage where people can transfer traditional money, like pounds or dollars, in exchange for cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or Ethereum. Most transactions are accompanied by fees. Binance is the world's biggest, which is part of what makes the hack so monumental. A crypto wallet is a place where investors hold their cryptocurrency. There are two types, a hot wallet and a cold wallet. Cold wallets are physical devices like specially designed USB sticks that store crypto offline typically for safer and longer term storage. Man told he can't recover £598m of Bitcoin from landfill site Ethereum is used to describe both the second largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, represented by the Ether token, and the blockchain underpinning it. This supports an array of different applications and digital assets, such as non-fungible tokens. It functions in a similar way to Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, but in 2022 switched to a greener operating system requiring less computers and energy . A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day. While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges. Cryptocurrency firm Terraform, behind the crashed TerraUSD and Luna tokens, files for bankruptcy XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation. This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value . The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves. These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand. So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean. While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it? Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions. This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers. Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam" . Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets. In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes. In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump. Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto. Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name. Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes. The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain. A crypto exchange is the digital platform where investors can buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies. Similar to traditional investing, a crypto exchange acts as a brokerage where people can transfer traditional money, like pounds or dollars, in exchange for cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or Ethereum. Most transactions are accompanied by fees. Binance is the world's biggest, which is part of what makes the hack so monumental. A crypto wallet is a place where investors hold their cryptocurrency. There are two types, a hot wallet and a cold wallet. Hot wallets are connected to the internet, and thus more accessible for quick transfers and easy access. Cold wallets are physical devices like specially designed USB sticks that store crypto offline typically for safer and longer term storage. Ethereum is used to describe both the second largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, represented by the Ether token, and the blockchain underpinning it. This supports an array of different applications and digital assets, such as non-fungible tokens. It functions in a similar way to Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, but in 2022 switched to a greener operating system requiring less computers and energy . ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies. A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day. While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges. Meme coins are a form of cryptocurrency used for fun and speculation. But meme coins are heavily criticised for their speculative nature and the risk involved for investors, as they often have little prospect of accumulating value over time. They can also be susceptible to "rug pulls" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers to raise the price of their coin, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales. Some celebrities have faced backlash after launching meme coins. Stablecoins themselves are usually controlled by companies that provide them, with transactions recorded on digital ledgers. While held up by some as the future of finance, high profile price collapses of stablecoins have alerted regulators to risks for investors and prompted scrutiny over their supposed stability. XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation. Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain. This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value .

extraction.body: From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance , the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines. The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves. These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand. So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean. While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it? Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions. This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers. Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam" . Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets. In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes. In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump. Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto. Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name. Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes. The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain. A crypto exchange is the digital platform where investors can buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies. Similar to traditional investing, a crypto exchange acts as a brokerage where people can transfer traditional money, like pounds or dollars, in exchange for cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or Ethereum. Most transactions are accompanied by fees. Binance is the world's biggest, which is part of what makes the hack so monumental. A crypto wallet is a place where investors hold their cryptocurrency. There are two types, a hot wallet and a cold wallet. Hot wallets are connected to the internet, and thus more accessible for quick transfers and easy access. Cold wallets are physical devices like specially designed USB sticks that store crypto offline typically for safer and longer term storage. Ethereum is used to describe both the second largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, represented by the Ether token, and the blockchain underpinning it. This supports an array of different applications and digital assets, such as non-fungible tokens. It functions in a similar way to Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, but in 2022 switched to a greener operating system requiring less computers and energy . ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies. A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day. While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges. Meme coins are a form of cryptocurrency used for fun and speculation. But meme coins are heavily criticised for their speculative nature and the risk involved for investors, as they often have little prospect of accumulating value over time. They can also be susceptible to "rug pulls" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers to raise the price of their coin, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales. Some celebrities have faced backlash after launching meme coins. Stablecoins themselves are usually controlled by companies that provide them, with transactions recorded on digital ledgers. While held up by some as the future of finance, high profile price collapses of stablecoins have alerted regulators to risks for investors and prompted scrutiny over their supposed stability. XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation. Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain. This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value .

extraction.body: On Thursday evening, I slipped on my neon yellow heels and a floral mini dress. It’s New York, so I can wear whatever I want to a midterm election event full of media types, techies, policy advocates, and, well, does anyone else even exist at these things? I walked into the dimly blue-lit Brooklyn warehouse and was surprised to see the room already filling up. Newsreel, the media company founded by former Forbes and Newsweek reporter Jack Brewster, hosted the event, and the lineup was heavy-hitting. Kenneth Schlenker, co-founder of the focus app Opal, sat down for a fireside chat about “the state of attention,” and Aryan Banjan, who built the campaign management software Barza, gave a midterm forecast. I, meanwhile, was moderating a panel on data centers. Brewster said the goal was for people to “put their phones away and talk to each other about the election, five days out.” As the evening progressed, however, one topic consumed nearly every conversation: AI, data centers, and the backlash against the growing technocracy. Lately, as a tech reporter, I’ve noticed a growing chasm between tech and everyone else. I spend most of my days talking to people who see the benefits of AI, who are so ambitious in building it and so optimistic that it will succeed that, when I talk to people beyond the tech world, I forget how ugly it all seems to them. Outside the tech bubble, data centers and AI have become such an intense ballot-box issue that they could sway some midterm races on November 3. A recent report from Data Center Watch found that almost $200 billion in data center projects were delayed, stalled, or blocked in the first half of 2026 due to political and community opposition. Meanwhile, states like Pennsylvania, Georgia, Texas, New York, and Virginia are considering more guardrails and transparency around data centers’ rapid development. Hundreds of new data centers are planned in Virginia alone, a state already nicknamed the “data center capital of the world.” A fireside chat with New York City Council member Chi Ossé, just before my panel, set the tone. AI came up near the end; Ossé said he doesn’t really use it. To me, though, he didn’t seem to be for or against it. He mostly emphasized that he would like to see tech executives held more accountable and trillionaires like Elon Musk taxed more. He described himself as a democratic socialist, but a “law and order” one. When CEOs talk about a technology that could deplete 10% of human civilization, he said, “they should be called to testify in front of Congress.” My panel was up next. I moderated a discussion with Maia Woluchem, a technology and human rights researcher, and Hilary Flint, an environmental and public health advocate, about data centers. As I took the stage, I decided to get a better read on the crowd. I asked, “Who here is pro-AI data center?” and was promptly booed. Our conversation covered a range of topics and emotions. People are upset that big tech companies appear to be cutting secret deals with local officials to build billion-dollar data centers. In some cases, zoning rules make it unclear what is being built until it’s too late to protest. At the same time, people are struggling with the cost of living and doing everything they can to hold onto what’s left of the American Dream, while tech leaders talk about AI replacing workers, or even humanity itself. Residents feel they have lost control over what happens in their communities, and they worry about the environmental and health risks. The panel agreed that data centers are the physical embodiment of people’s fears and anger toward the tech class and the rapid pace of technology. “What is a life worth?” Flint said when I brought up the benefits that some communities have seen from data center build-outs. People still protest, she said, because they “value their lives a little bit more than a temporary check.” The panel after mine featured NewsNation host Batya Ungar-Sargon; political strategist Morris Katz, who worked on Zohran Mamdani’s campaign; and Vox’s Astead Herndon. They were supposed to be talking about the future of the Democratic Party. But once again, the conversation shifted to data centers. Ungar-Sargon noted that some labor unions support data centers because of the jobs they promise. (Reports show that data centers create many jobs initially, but those jobs are not permanent once construction ends.) “There used to be a lot of pride in a community in the Rust Belt about very ugly, enormous buildings in their communities because everybody worked there,” she said, nodding to an earlier comment I’d made about data centers being ugly. “And they knew that building represented prosperity for themselves, stability for their children, and a future and a piece of the American dream.” Herndon noted that Vivek Ramaswamy was booed for making a similar point in Ohio, a Rust Belt state. “I just want to reinforce the lack of consent happening,” he said. “Because that’s true among Republicans in those places and I’ve watched it.” Katz was also skeptical. “It’s the same people who have taken so many union jobs away,” he said. “The same institutional powers that have robbed labor and working people of jobs and profit. Now coming back to essentially finish the job and take whatever scraps remain.” Along the warehouse walls, I noticed sticky notes answering posted questions, including “Will we ever be able to get Big Money out of politics?” “God, I hope so,” one note said. People rushed the bar when the panel ended, and techno music began to blast. They broke into small groups, where AI and data centers were once again the topic, this time in more private conversations. I asked Brewster if he was surprised by how much of the conversation focused on AI and data centers. “It came up in every conversation on stage, and it was the second most common topic in the questions people sent us when they RSVP’d,” he said, adding that it was happening even in New York, where data centers aren’t very visible. “AI has become an election issue for regular voters,” he said. “In rural communities, the backlash is about feeling replaced. In a place like Brooklyn, it’s more about who gets rich from it.” Before leaving, I made the rounds, asking people to name the craziest thing they’d seen in tech this year. Two tech founders mentioned the AI assistant startup Instinct, while a non-tech person named Sam Altman Another non-tech person brought up the rise of deepfakes and AI art. AI art, she said, is starting to signal cheapness. That may be why luxury brands are going the other way: Prada’s holiday campaign features hand-drawn illustrations , and Hermès has been spotlighting artists’ handmade work on Instagram. On my way out, I spoke to a software engineer who said the craziest thing she’d seen this year was a person who painted their nails orange for Halloween and was asked if it was a tribute to the Anthropic IPO. I admitted that I, too, had once worn a burnt orange dress and briefly thought of myself as the Claude logo. She later told me data centers are popping up in her Southern California hometown, too. Hearing that, I thought for the first time about how I’d feel if one popped up in mine. She grew up in a Chinese immigrant community, where neighbors are putting signs in their yards showing dragons choking a data center. The signs have since been translated into other languages, she said.

“There is this little issue that I recently started hearing about that I wanted to tell you about, in case you don’t know,” Hinojosa quipped to a Democratic Party-organized crowd of about 160 seated on fold-out chairs at an Amarillo social club in Texas’ panhandle.
“They’ll just hit that button, Republican all the way down,” Bertrand said.
“But I think it’s a step towards something that we have not seen in Texas in a long time, with people on the right switching to the left.
Or scooting a little closer to the middle, maybe.”

Rumors are flying about others popping up — Google, which is building four data centers in northwest Texas, sponsored moderated conversations with officials and business elite in Lubbock and Amarillo in recent weeks — and it is sowing an outcry across small cities, tiny towns and sprawling ranches where people vote overwhelmingly Republican.
Democrats are prominent among the data center critics, but so are Republicans, including Texas’ sitting agriculture commissioner, Sid Miller.
They say there are many more Republicans who are quieter because they fear publicly opposing their governor and party.

Texas is increasingly steamrolling over landowner rights in the quest for public water, Dalby said, and that could mean that data centers get in line ahead of ranchers when shortages or rationing worsen.

At an East Texas campaign stop , Abbott said that includes taking away the state’s billion-dollar-plus-per-year tax break and preventing data centers from being built in “rural Texas neighborhoods.”

It has lots of land, lots of energy and a friendly regulatory environment under Republican leadership.
Some come with designs for natural gas-fired turbines to power them.

Compounding that, Texas counties don’t have zoning authority — precisely the local land planning authority that communities around the country are increasingly using to fight off data centers.
“Oh, I guarantee you, it’s on everybody’s mind,” said Giles Dalby, a cattle rancher and a Republican county commissioner in west Texas.

The big question is whether enough rural voters will turn against Abbott to give Hinojosa a shot.
It’s hard to tell, Bertrand said, especially when some know nothing about the issue.

Others say construction and an influx of workers are already causing havoc for ranchers and towns, driving up rents, snapping up farmland, illuminating the night sky, clogging roads and turning parts of rural Texas into industrial zones.

extraction.body: On Thursday evening, I slipped on my neon yellow heels and a floral mini dress. It’s New York, so I can wear whatever I want to a midterm election event full of media types, techies, policy advocates, and, well, does anyone else even exist at these things? I walked into the dimly blue-lit Brooklyn warehouse and was surprised to see the room already filling up. Newsreel, the media company founded by former Forbes and Newsweek reporter Jack Brewster, hosted the event, and the lineup was heavy-hitting. Kenneth Schlenker, co-founder of the focus app Opal, sat down for a fireside chat about “the state of attention,” and Aryan Banjan, who built the campaign management software Barza, gave a midterm forecast. I, meanwhile, was moderating a panel on data centers. Brewster said the goal was for people to “put their phones away and talk to each other about the election, five days out.” As the evening progressed, however, one topic consumed nearly every conversation: AI, data centers, and the backlash against the growing technocracy. Lately, as a tech reporter, I’ve noticed a growing chasm between tech and everyone else. I spend most of my days talking to people who see the benefits of AI, who are so ambitious in building it and so optimistic that it will succeed that, when I talk to people beyond the tech world, I forget how ugly it all seems to them. Outside the tech bubble, data centers and AI have become such an intense ballot-box issue that they could sway some midterm races on November 3. A recent report from Data Center Watch found that almost $200 billion in data center projects were delayed, stalled, or blocked in the first half of 2026 due to political and community opposition. Meanwhile, states like Pennsylvania, Georgia, Texas, New York, and Virginia are considering more guardrails and transparency around data centers’ rapid development. Hundreds of new data centers are planned in Virginia alone, a state already nicknamed the “data center capital of the world.” A fireside chat with New York City Council member Chi Ossé, just before my panel, set the tone. AI came up near the end; Ossé said he doesn’t really use it. To me, though, he didn’t seem to be for or against it. He mostly emphasized that he would like to see tech executives held more accountable and trillionaires like Elon Musk taxed more. He described himself as a democratic socialist, but a “law and order” one. When CEOs talk about a technology that could deplete 10% of human civilization, he said, “they should be called to testify in front of Congress.” My panel was up next. I moderated a discussion with Maia Woluchem, a technology and human rights researcher, and Hilary Flint, an environmental and public health advocate, about data centers. As I took the stage, I decided to get a better read on the crowd. I asked, “Who here is pro-AI data center?” and was promptly booed. Our conversation covered a range of topics and emotions. People are upset that big tech companies appear to be cutting secret deals with local officials to build billion-dollar data centers. In some cases, zoning rules make it unclear what is being built until it’s too late to protest. At the same time, people are struggling with the cost of living and doing everything they can to hold onto what’s left of the American Dream, while tech leaders talk about AI replacing workers, or even humanity itself. Residents feel they have lost control over what happens in their communities, and they worry about the environmental and health risks. The panel agreed that data centers are the physical embodiment of people’s fears and anger toward the tech class and the rapid pace of technology. “What is a life worth?” Flint said when I brought up the benefits that some communities have seen from data center build-outs. People still protest, she said, because they “value their lives a little bit more than a temporary check.” The panel after mine featured NewsNation host Batya Ungar-Sargon; political strategist Morris Katz, who worked on Zohran Mamdani’s campaign; and Vox’s Astead Herndon. They were supposed to be talking about the future of the Democratic Party. But once again, the conversation shifted to data centers. Ungar-Sargon noted that some labor unions support data centers because of the jobs they promise. (Reports show that data centers create many jobs initially, but those jobs are not permanent once construction ends.) “There used to be a lot of pride in a community in the Rust Belt about very ugly, enormous buildings in their communities because everybody worked there,” she said, nodding to an earlier comment I’d made about data centers being ugly. “And they knew that building represented prosperity for themselves, stability for their children, and a future and a piece of the American dream.” Herndon noted that Vivek Ramaswamy was booed for making a similar point in Ohio, a Rust Belt state. “I just want to reinforce the lack of consent happening,” he said. “Because that’s true among Republicans in those places and I’ve watched it.” Katz was also skeptical. “It’s the same people who have taken so many union jobs away,” he said. “The same institutional powers that have robbed labor and working people of jobs and profit. Now coming back to essentially finish the job and take whatever scraps remain.” Along the warehouse walls, I noticed sticky notes answering posted questions, including “Will we ever be able to get Big Money out of politics?” “God, I hope so,” one note said. People rushed the bar when the panel ended, and techno music began to blast. They broke into small groups, where AI and data centers were once again the topic, this time in more private conversations. I asked Brewster if he was surprised by how much of the conversation focused on AI and data centers. “It came up in every conversation on stage, and it was the second most common topic in the questions people sent us when they RSVP’d,” he said, adding that it was happening even in New York, where data centers aren’t very visible. “AI has become an election issue for regular voters,” he said. “In rural communities, the backlash is about feeling replaced. In a place like Brooklyn, it’s more about who gets rich from it.” Before leaving, I made the rounds, asking people to name the craziest thing they’d seen in tech this year. Two tech founders mentioned the AI assistant startup Instinct, while a non-tech person named Sam Altman Another non-tech person brought up the rise of deepfakes and AI art. AI art, she said, is starting to signal cheapness. That may be why luxury brands are going the other way: Prada’s holiday campaign features hand-drawn illustrations , and Hermès has been spotlighting artists’ handmade work on Instagram. On my way out, I spoke to a software engineer who said the craziest thing she’d seen this year was a person who painted their nails orange for Halloween and was asked if it was a tribute to the Anthropic IPO. I admitted that I, too, had once worn a burnt orange dress and briefly thought of myself as the Claude logo. She later told me data centers are popping up in her Southern California hometown, too. Hearing that, I thought for the first time about how I’d feel if one popped up in mine. She grew up in a Chinese immigrant community, where neighbors are putting signs in their yards showing dragons choking a data center. The signs have since been translated into other languages, she said.

But with barely three months until November’s contest, the perceived threat to rural life, ranchland and dwindling water supplies could become a defining issue for her long-shot challenge to Republican Gov. Greg Abbott , dividing conservative rural areas that have traditionally served as a counterweight to Democrats’ urban strongholds. The backlash to energy-guzzling server warehouses is also shaping other statewide campaigns from Arizona to Ohio to New York, and even giving Democrats a glimmer of hope in Texas, where Republicans have dominated for three decades. “There is this little issue that I recently started hearing about that I wanted to tell you about, in case you don’t know,” Hinojosa quipped to a Democratic Party-organized crowd of about 160 seated on fold-out chairs at an Amarillo social club in Texas’ panhandle. “It’s this issue of data centers.” The crowd booed, and she went on: “They are owned by the richest men in the world. We’re all footing the bill. There are no rules. It is the wild west of data centers.” The fast growth of massive data centers has already upended races for local offices across the country, often uniting conservatives and liberals in revolting against projects in their midst. Now the ripple effects have spread to top-of-the-ticket races, where incumbents and challengers are trying to show that they hear an angry electorate. In Ohio, Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown aired a television advertisement attacking Republican U.S. Sen. John Husted as the “face of data centers in Ohio” as people gather signatures for a statewide referendum to outright ban their construction. In Wisconsin, a Democratic candidate for governor, Francesca Hong , is pledging to “tax the rich, fund our schools and stop AI data centers” as she campaigns for her party’s nomination in a crowded primary. In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro is facing heat from some voters who feel like he’s been too welcoming to tech behemoths . Sam Burleigh, a Democrat whose rural community is fighting off data center projects, accused Shapiro of “allowing these data centers to come in and take over acres and acres of prime farmland.” The state is poised to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a report by commercial real estate giant JLL. It has lots of land, lots of energy and a friendly regulatory environment under Republican leadership. In rural west Texas and its panhandle, gargantuan data centers are under construction, including one near Amarillo touted as the world’s largest. Some come with designs for natural gas-fired turbines to power them. Rumors are flying about others popping up — Google, which is building four data centers in northwest Texas, sponsored moderated conversations with officials and business elite in Lubbock and Amarillo in recent weeks — and it is sowing an outcry across small cities, tiny towns and sprawling ranches where people vote overwhelmingly Republican. Google says its investments are advancing American innovation, fortifying cybersecurity and boosting energy capacity , while President Donald Trump has made data centers a top priority to help the U.S. compete against China for AI superiority . But tech giants and developers can be secretive about their plans, making it impossible to know what will be built or what sort of pollution they’ll create, critics say. Some worry that data centers will destroy rural Texas’ low cost of living and sully sunsets and sweeping views that stretch toward the horizon. Others say construction and an influx of workers are already causing havoc for ranchers and towns, driving up rents, snapping up farmland, illuminating the night sky, clogging roads and turning parts of rural Texas into industrial zones. Democrats are prominent among the data center critics, but so are Republicans, including Texas’ sitting agriculture commissioner, Sid Miller. They say there are many more Republicans who are quieter because they fear publicly opposing their governor and party. “They’re upset with Greg Abbott,” said Suzanne Bellsnyder, a former Republican activist from Spearman who writes a syndicated column that advocates for rural Texas. “Whether that translates into voting against him, I don’t know.” Abbott has aggressively advocated for big projects in Texas and, in November, he helped make Google’s announcement of a $40 billion investment there, saying “Texas is the epicenter of AI development.” Compounding that, Texas counties don’t have zoning authority — precisely the local land planning authority that communities around the country are increasingly using to fight off data centers. Abbott seems to recognize that data centers are dividing his base. In recent weeks, he ordered regulators to take steps to ensure Texans weren’t paying higher electricity bills because of data centers and promised to push a legislative agenda next year to impose regulations on data centers. At an East Texas campaign stop , Abbott said that includes taking away the state’s billion-dollar-plus-per-year tax break and preventing data centers from being built in “rural Texas neighborhoods.” Hinojosa and others derided Abbott’s words about “rural Texas neighborhoods” as meaningless — “doublespeak that makes no sense to anyone,” Hinojosa said — and lacking urgency or seriousness. “Now we have this gold rush of data centers in our communities,” Hinojosa said in an interview, adding that “people want a say, and I think that’s fair.” As governor, she said she’d block a permit for a data center if it wasn’t a good deal for Texans or residents hadn’t gotten a say in the matter. Abbott’s campaign season turnabout on data centers doesn’t seem to have soothed many. Dalby, who raises Angus and Brangus cattle on ranchland that’s been in his family for 125 years, pointed to fast-growing cities where water authorities have had to go to greater lengths to procure water, including the “water wars” between San Antonio and ranchers several years ago. Texas is increasingly steamrolling over landowner rights in the quest for public water, Dalby said, and that could mean that data centers get in line ahead of ranchers when shortages or rationing worsen. Clayton Tucker, a rancher and the Democratic nominee for state agriculture commissioner, said his campaign events are consumed by talk of data centers. It doesn’t matter whether he’s meeting with Democrats or Republicans. “This is the most cross-partisan issue I’ve ever seen in my life,” Tucker said. Meanwhile, protest groups are springing up, including one in Lubbock that is led by Republicans. The founders, Stephen Sanders and Hallie Bertrand, like some other Republican opponents of data centers, say it’s possible or even certain they won’t vote for Abbott, although they may not necessarily vote for Hinojosa. There is still time for Abbott to push through major legislation before the election and “be a hero,” Sanders said. The big question is whether enough rural voters will turn against Abbott to give Hinojosa a shot. It’s hard to tell, Bertrand said, especially when some know nothing about the issue. “They’ll just hit that button, Republican all the way down,” Bertrand said. “But I think it’s a step towards something that we have not seen in Texas in a long time, with people on the right switching to the left. Or scooting a little closer to the middle, maybe.”

extraction.body: FBI says North Korea behind $6 billion crypto theft from Binance The FBI on Saturday accused North Korea of stealing more than $6 billion in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance in what is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist. The US law enforcement agency's statement came as Binance offered reassurances it was covering the losses from the hacking attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90 percent of what was stolen. Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the cyberattack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday. The FBI confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack. TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year. "The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said. The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services. It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets." US President Donald Trump, however, cast doubt on the North Korea's involvement in the hack. "I'm not concerned. We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea," Trump told reporters at his residence in Florida late Saturday. The president often reflects with pride on summits he held with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term. Binance said Saturday it has set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in the hack. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X. It said it has used company money to buy tokens to replenish 90 percent of the stolen funds, while the remaining 10 percent of tokens are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts." Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said in its latest update they were on track to resume Sunday. The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols. Bitcoin plunged nearly five percent after the news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly six percent and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 percent. Binance said Friday it was working to resolve what it called a "complex attack" with several "points of breach." The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea -- which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programs -- to find illicit means to capture revenue. TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview," a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim.

The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services. It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets." extraction.body: Salt and vinegar chips, in my opinion, are one of the most divisive snacks out there. People either love that sharp, acidic punch or want absolutely nothing to do with it. I am firmly in the first camp, which is why I rounded up every bag I could find to see which brand makes the best ones. My ideal salt and vinegar chip is so aggressively vinegary that it practically makes my eyes water, but for this taste test, I tried to show a little restraint. The best chip is balanced: enough acidity to make your mouth pucker, plenty of salt, a strong potato flavor, and, most importantly, a chip sturdy enough to handle it all. I tried seven popular brands—Lay’s, Siete, Utz, Kettle Brand, Cape Cod, Deep River, and Pringles—to find the one that does salt and vinegar best. Here’s how they ranked. Utz came out swinging with plenty of sour flavor, but unfortunately, that was about the only thing I enjoyed. The texture was my biggest issue. Instead of that clean, crisp crunch I want from a potato chip, these had an almost powdery quality that made each bite feel oddly dry. The seasoning was intensely acidic, but not in the bright, vinegary way I usually love. It built quickly into a harsh sourness that became almost nauseating after a few chips. Looking at the ingredient list, the seasoning relies on sodium diacetate along with several acids, and I could really taste that concentrated acidity. I love a powerful salt and vinegar chip, but this one crossed the line from punchy into overwhelming. Pringles Salt & Vinegar taste exactly like what you would expect: a familiar Pringles base with a tangy layer of vinegar seasoning. The flavor is pleasant, with a mild acidic bite and enough salt to make it clearly salt and vinegar. My problem is with the chip underneath. For this particular flavor, I want an actual potato chip with enough heft and crunch to stand up against all that acidity—not a potato-based crisp. If you already love Pringles, you’ll probably enjoy these. They just weren’t what I was personally looking for in this test. Siete immediately won points for texture. These have a great, substantial crunch, and the avocado oil imparts a mild flavor that lets the potato shine. What I didn't like was the serrano. The added pepper brings a mild vegetal heat that competes with the vinegar instead of letting it be the star. A noticeable salty tang still comes through, but I kept wishing I could taste more of it without the serrano getting in the way. Still, the crunch and vinegar were good enough to land these safely above the bottom two. The thin chip is light and crispy, and the potato itself tastes better than Utz. The seasoning has a clean, familiar salt and vinegar flavor with a pleasant sharpness that hits right away. For a flavor this bold, Lay’s felt a little too polite. The vinegar fades quickly, leaving you mostly with the salty potato chip underneath. These are extremely easy to eat, but if I’m buying salt and vinegar chips, I want the vinegar to make itself known. Deep River delivered the first truly satisfying vinegar punch of the group. The acidity hits immediately, but it comes across slightly sweeter and rounder than some of the sharper chips in this ranking. That little touch of sweetness softens the sourness without eliminating it, and the seasoning lingers nicely after each bite. The kettle-cooked texture also gives these the sturdy crunch this flavor needs. They weren’t quite as balanced as my top two, but I appreciated that Deep River wasn’t afraid of vinegar. Kettle Brand came extremely close to taking the top spot. The chips have a fantastic crunch: thick and substantial without becoming painfully hard. The vinegar flavor is bright, acidic, and immediately satisfying, with enough salt to make the whole thing pop. My only complaint is how quickly the seasoning disappears. The first few seconds of each bite are exactly what I want from salt and vinegar, but once that initial tang fades, you’re mostly left with a plain potato chip. Apparently that didn’t bother me too much, because I kept reaching back into the bag. That is usually a pretty reliable sign that a chip is doing something right. Cape Cod gave me the best overall combination of crunch, salt, potato, and vinegar. These have a bold kettle-cooked crunch that immediately makes them feel more substantial, followed by a vinegar flavor that is bright and tangy without becoming harsh. I could personally handle even more acidity, but the balance here is what ultimately earned them first place. The seasoning includes both white vinegar and apple cider vinegar, and I think that combination really sets these apart. The white vinegar gives you that clean acidic bite, while the apple cider vinegar adds a slightly fruitier, more rounded tang that gives the overall flavor more depth. Delish Test Kitchen Manager Alejandro Valdes Lora agreed, praising the great texture and fresh, crisp, slightly oily potato-chip flavor. He even went so far as to declare that Cape Cod “never disappoints.” I couldn’t agree more. After eating my way through seven bags, one thing became very clear: Kettle-cooked chips are the ideal vehicle for salt and vinegar. A flavor this strong needs a substantial potato chip underneath it. The thicker crunch gives all that sharp vinegar and salt something to push against, creating a much more satisfying bite. And while I will always support a chip acidic enough to make me tear up, Cape Cod proved that sometimes balance wins. Think You Can't Bake? extraction.body: Welcome to Dupe Detective, a column where I'll be reviewing a name brand food product's competitor product to find out how well it compares to, or even beats, the original. Despite a famously bold, sometimes mouth-numbing flavor, salt and vinegar chips are surprisingly versatile. Starbucks salt and vinegar chips, for example, can be paired with coffee for a combo as satisfying as it is unconventional. In another instance of chain restaurant chip innovation, Red Lobster once added salt and vinegar chips to breaded shrimp . Simply put, there's something distinctly gratifying about a robust vinegary tang amplified by almost too much salt on crispy potato that has inspired these and other adventurous eats. Kettle has arguably become one America's most beloved potato chip brands , producing what may well be the most iconic salt and vinegar chip available in grocery stores. Competing directly with Kettle Chips is Trader Joes, which sells Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips with Avocado Oil. The Trader Joe's product even comes in a blue bag, reminiscent of the equivalent Kettle Chips packaging. I picked both brands' takes on the classic chip flavor from stores near my home in the suburbs of Las Vegas and tried them back-to-back. Ahead is a brief rundown of each item, before my thoughts on how Trader Joe's holds up against its name-brand competition. While the info isn't spotlighted on the front of the bag, Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips are, in fact, kettle-cooked. One of the foremost qualities that sets kettle-cooked chips apart from standard potato chips is their pronounced crunch, which is satisfying on its own, or even swapped into a nacho recipe for the crunchiest take on nachos possible. My Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips were certainly crunchy, and I noticed they were the slightest bit thicker than the average potato chip too. In other words, I had nothing but positive thoughts about my Trader Joe's chips' texture. Foremost in my Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chips' flavor was malt vinegar. The fact I could taste that malty sweetness, more complex than a plain white vinegar, was a significant plus. Whereas some salt and vinegar chips are so bold they cause a tingling sensation from the get-go, I did notice a certain level of restraint from Trader Joe's — it took maybe a few pinch-fuls of chips before I started noticing that signature buildup up salty tang. Finally, rounding out my Trader Joe's experience was a potato flavor I found closer to that of a french fry than, say, a more vegetal baked potato. While the distinction was subtle, it was a quality I appreciated all the same. Had I compared Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chip and their Kettle Chips equivalent in a more casual setting, I likely would have found them difficult to distinguish from one another. With that said, I did pick up on a few subtle differences after a deep dive on both products. First off, while extra thickness is part of what sets Kettle Chips apart from regular potato chips , I thought my Trader Joe's chips were just the slightest bit thicker, whereas my name-brand Kettle Chips were a tad airier. That meant the former remained crunchy for a little longer, whereas my Kettle Chips' crunch wore off faster. In the flavor department, I found Kettle Chips' ratio of its two core ingredients slightly higher in salt — vinegar dominated the experience of my Trader Joe's chips, while the Kettle Chips formula featured salt and vinegar in roughly equivalent quantities. I also found Kettle Chips' vinegar flavor simpler, closer to a straight-up white vinegar. Plus, I picked up the slightest vegetal flavor from their potato component, contrasting with the more fried potato character of my Trader Joe's chips. Over time, I also noticed that the vinegar flavor had a tendency to fade, leaving a less complex salty potato aftertaste. There's no wrong choice between Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips and Seal Salt & Vinegar Kettle Chips — anyone craving a high-quality salt and vinegar chip would probably find both products satisfying. Nevertheless, true tingly chip-heads looking for the very best salt and vinegar chips on grocery store shelves should pick Trader Joe's over Kettle Chips. Previously, Trader Joe's Baked Cheese Crunchies beat Cheetos in a head-to-head , so for what it's worth, Trader Joe's remains a heavy hitter in the snack department. The qualities I preferred in my Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips included their pronounced crunch, a more complex malt vinegar that lingered longer, and a fried potato flavor. For clarity's sake, those were all subtle elements that I was able to identify because my critical brain was actively looking for them, as opposed to glaring differences. That said, those differences were significant enough that, with both products in my pantry for a few days, I really only ever snacked on the Trader Joe's chips –leaving the slightly inferior Kettle Chips practically untouched. As much as both products are solid, then, it's fair to say that Trader Joe's makes the superior salt and vinegar chip. At my local Trader Joe's, in the Las Vegas-adjacent Henderson, Nevada, a 7-ounce bag of Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips is $2.99. At an Albertsons between that Trader Joe's and my home, a 7.5-ounce bag of Seal Salt & Vinegar Kettle Chips is $4.29. Nutritionally, a 1-ounce serving of Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips totals 140 calories, 7 grams of fat, 1 gram of which is saturated fat, 200 milligrams of sodium, 17 grams of carbs, 1 gram of fiber, and 2 grams of protein. An equivalent 1-ounce serving of salt and vinegar Kettle Chips equals 140 calories, 9 grams of fat, 1 gram of which is saturated fat, 180 milligrams of sodium, 15 grams of carbs, 2 grams of fiber, and 2 grams of protein. Altogether, then, the Trader Joe's chips are quite a bit cheaper but technically higher in sodium and carbs — those latter numbers, however, are minor enough to consider negligible. I picked up my Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips from one of the two stores closest to my home in the suburbs of Las Vegas, and then stopped at an Albertsons on the way back to my house for my bag of Seal Salt & Vinegar Kettle Chips. Since both products are meant to be enjoyed at room temperature, I tried them both pretty much as soon as I was home. I started with a few Trader Joe's chips, noting down my thoughts on their texture and flavor as I ate. Then I did the same with a few Kettle Chips. After I recorded my initial impressions, I alternated more of each kind of chip in order to better understand the qualities that set them apart from one another. Over the course of the next few days, I snacked on some leftover chips, and I made sure to keep my critical brain slightly active to ensure my impressions held up over time. My assessments are based entirely on this experience and not any past thoughts I may have had on the featured brands or products.

extraction.body: Salt and vinegar chips, in my opinion, are one of the most divisive snacks out there. People either love that sharp, acidic punch or want absolutely nothing to do with it. I am firmly in the first camp, which is why I rounded up every bag I could find to see which brand makes the best ones. My ideal salt and vinegar chip is so aggressively vinegary that it practically makes my eyes water, but for this taste test, I tried to show a little restraint. The best chip is balanced: enough acidity to make your mouth pucker, plenty of salt, a strong potato flavor, and, most importantly, a chip sturdy enough to handle it all. I tried seven popular brands—Lay’s, Siete, Utz, Kettle Brand, Cape Cod, Deep River, and Pringles—to find the one that does salt and vinegar best. Here’s how they ranked. Utz came out swinging with plenty of sour flavor, but unfortunately, that was about the only thing I enjoyed. The texture was my biggest issue. Instead of that clean, crisp crunch I want from a potato chip, these had an almost powdery quality that made each bite feel oddly dry. The seasoning was intensely acidic, but not in the bright, vinegary way I usually love. It built quickly into a harsh sourness that became almost nauseating after a few chips. Looking at the ingredient list, the seasoning relies on sodium diacetate along with several acids, and I could really taste that concentrated acidity. I love a powerful salt and vinegar chip, but this one crossed the line from punchy into overwhelming. Pringles Salt & Vinegar taste exactly like what you would expect: a familiar Pringles base with a tangy layer of vinegar seasoning. The flavor is pleasant, with a mild acidic bite and enough salt to make it clearly salt and vinegar. My problem is with the chip underneath. For this particular flavor, I want an actual potato chip with enough heft and crunch to stand up against all that acidity—not a potato-based crisp. If you already love Pringles, you’ll probably enjoy these. They just weren’t what I was personally looking for in this test. Siete immediately won points for texture. These have a great, substantial crunch, and the avocado oil imparts a mild flavor that lets the potato shine. What I didn't like was the serrano. The added pepper brings a mild vegetal heat that competes with the vinegar instead of letting it be the star. A noticeable salty tang still comes through, but I kept wishing I could taste more of it without the serrano getting in the way. Still, the crunch and vinegar were good enough to land these safely above the bottom two. The thin chip is light and crispy, and the potato itself tastes better than Utz. The seasoning has a clean, familiar salt and vinegar flavor with a pleasant sharpness that hits right away. For a flavor this bold, Lay’s felt a little too polite. The vinegar fades quickly, leaving you mostly with the salty potato chip underneath. These are extremely easy to eat, but if I’m buying salt and vinegar chips, I want the vinegar to make itself known. Deep River delivered the first truly satisfying vinegar punch of the group. The acidity hits immediately, but it comes across slightly sweeter and rounder than some of the sharper chips in this ranking. That little touch of sweetness softens the sourness without eliminating it, and the seasoning lingers nicely after each bite. The kettle-cooked texture also gives these the sturdy crunch this flavor needs. They weren’t quite as balanced as my top two, but I appreciated that Deep River wasn’t afraid of vinegar. Kettle Brand came extremely close to taking the top spot. The chips have a fantastic crunch: thick and substantial without becoming painfully hard. The vinegar flavor is bright, acidic, and immediately satisfying, with enough salt to make the whole thing pop. My only complaint is how quickly the seasoning disappears. The first few seconds of each bite are exactly what I want from salt and vinegar, but once that initial tang fades, you’re mostly left with a plain potato chip. Apparently that didn’t bother me too much, because I kept reaching back into the bag. That is usually a pretty reliable sign that a chip is doing something right. Cape Cod gave me the best overall combination of crunch, salt, potato, and vinegar. These have a bold kettle-cooked crunch that immediately makes them feel more substantial, followed by a vinegar flavor that is bright and tangy without becoming harsh. I could personally handle even more acidity, but the balance here is what ultimately earned them first place. The seasoning includes both white vinegar and apple cider vinegar, and I think that combination really sets these apart. The white vinegar gives you that clean acidic bite, while the apple cider vinegar adds a slightly fruitier, more rounded tang that gives the overall flavor more depth. Delish Test Kitchen Manager Alejandro Valdes Lora agreed, praising the great texture and fresh, crisp, slightly oily potato-chip flavor. He even went so far as to declare that Cape Cod “never disappoints.” I couldn’t agree more. After eating my way through seven bags, one thing became very clear: Kettle-cooked chips are the ideal vehicle for salt and vinegar. A flavor this strong needs a substantial potato chip underneath it. The thicker crunch gives all that sharp vinegar and salt something to push against, creating a much more satisfying bite. And while I will always support a chip acidic enough to make me tear up, Cape Cod proved that sometimes balance wins. Think You Can't Bake? extraction.body: Welcome to Dupe Detective, a column where I'll be reviewing a name brand food product's competitor product to find out how well it compares to, or even beats, the original. Despite a famously bold, sometimes mouth-numbing flavor, salt and vinegar chips are surprisingly versatile. Starbucks salt and vinegar chips, for example, can be paired with coffee for a combo as satisfying as it is unconventional. In another instance of chain restaurant chip innovation, Red Lobster once added salt and vinegar chips to breaded shrimp . Simply put, there's something distinctly gratifying about a robust vinegary tang amplified by almost too much salt on crispy potato that has inspired these and other adventurous eats. Kettle has arguably become one America's most beloved potato chip brands , producing what may well be the most iconic salt and vinegar chip available in grocery stores. Competing directly with Kettle Chips is Trader Joes, which sells Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips with Avocado Oil. The Trader Joe's product even comes in a blue bag, reminiscent of the equivalent Kettle Chips packaging. I picked both brands' takes on the classic chip flavor from stores near my home in the suburbs of Las Vegas and tried them back-to-back. Ahead is a brief rundown of each item, before my thoughts on how Trader Joe's holds up against its name-brand competition. While the info isn't spotlighted on the front of the bag, Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips are, in fact, kettle-cooked. One of the foremost qualities that sets kettle-cooked chips apart from standard potato chips is their pronounced crunch, which is satisfying on its own, or even swapped into a nacho recipe for the crunchiest take on nachos possible. My Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips were certainly crunchy, and I noticed they were the slightest bit thicker than the average potato chip too. In other words, I had nothing but positive thoughts about my Trader Joe's chips' texture. Foremost in my Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chips' flavor was malt vinegar. The fact I could taste that malty sweetness, more complex than a plain white vinegar, was a significant plus. Whereas some salt and vinegar chips are so bold they cause a tingling sensation from the get-go, I did notice a certain level of restraint from Trader Joe's — it took maybe a few pinch-fuls of chips before I started noticing that signature buildup up salty tang. Finally, rounding out my Trader Joe's experience was a potato flavor I found closer to that of a french fry than, say, a more vegetal baked potato. While the distinction was subtle, it was a quality I appreciated all the same. Had I compared Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chip and their Kettle Chips equivalent in a more casual setting, I likely would have found them difficult to distinguish from one another. With that said, I did pick up on a few subtle differences after a deep dive on both products. First off, while extra thickness is part of what sets Kettle Chips apart from regular potato chips , I thought my Trader Joe's chips were just the slightest bit thicker, whereas my name-brand Kettle Chips were a tad airier. That meant the former remained crunchy for a little longer, whereas my Kettle Chips' crunch wore off faster. In the flavor department, I found Kettle Chips' ratio of its two core ingredients slightly higher in salt — vinegar dominated the experience of my Trader Joe's chips, while the Kettle Chips formula featured salt and vinegar in roughly equivalent quantities. I also found Kettle Chips' vinegar flavor simpler, closer to a straight-up white vinegar. Plus, I picked up the slightest vegetal flavor from their potato component, contrasting with the more fried potato character of my Trader Joe's chips. Over time, I also noticed that the vinegar flavor had a tendency to fade, leaving a less complex salty potato aftertaste. There's no wrong choice between Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips and Seal Salt & Vinegar Kettle Chips — anyone craving a high-quality salt and vinegar chip would probably find both products satisfying. Nevertheless, true tingly chip-heads looking for the very best salt and vinegar chips on grocery store shelves should pick Trader Joe's over Kettle Chips. Previously, Trader Joe's Baked Cheese Crunchies beat Cheetos in a head-to-head , so for what it's worth, Trader Joe's remains a heavy hitter in the snack department. The qualities I preferred in my Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips included their pronounced crunch, a more complex malt vinegar that lingered longer, and a fried potato flavor. For clarity's sake, those were all subtle elements that I was able to identify because my critical brain was actively looking for them, as opposed to glaring differences. That said, those differences were significant enough that, with both products in my pantry for a few days, I really only ever snacked on the Trader Joe's chips –leaving the slightly inferior Kettle Chips practically untouched. As much as both products are solid, then, it's fair to say that Trader Joe's makes the superior salt and vinegar chip. Despite a famously bold, sometimes mouth-numbing flavor, salt and vinegar chips are surprisingly versatile. Starbucks salt and vinegar chips, for example, can be paired with coffee for a combo as satisfying as it is unconventional. In another instance of chain restaurant chip innovation, Red Lobster once added salt and vinegar chips to breaded shrimp . Simply put, there's something distinctly gratifying about a robust vinegary tang amplified by almost too much salt on crispy potato that has inspired these and other adventurous eats.

Kettle has arguably become one America's most beloved potato chip brands , producing what may well be the most iconic salt and vinegar chip available in grocery stores. Competing directly with Kettle Chips is Trader Joes, which sells Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips with Avocado Oil. The Trader Joe's product even comes in a blue bag, reminiscent of the equivalent Kettle Chips packaging. I picked both brands' takes on the classic chip flavor from stores near my home in the suburbs of Las Vegas and tried them back-to-back. Ahead is a brief rundown of each item, before my thoughts on how Trader Joe's holds up against its name-brand competition.

While the info isn't spotlighted on the front of the bag, Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips are, in fact, kettle-cooked. One of the foremost qualities that sets kettle-cooked chips apart from standard potato chips is their pronounced crunch, which is satisfying on its own, or even swapped into a nacho recipe for the crunchiest take on nachos possible. In other words, I had nothing but positive thoughts about my Trader Joe's chips' texture.

The incident occurred during a homecoming football game on Friday night (October 2) , police said, according to CBS News.Authorities responded to the incident outside Aerie Stadium on the school's north side around 8:40 pm. Police said the two wounded persons, whose ages have not been revealed, were taken to the hospital with injuries that were not life-threatening. Law enforcement personnel from nearby communities also responded to the emergency and had secured the area by 9:22 pm, according to Eden Prairie Local News (EPLN).No arrests made so farEden Prairie Police Chief Matt Sacket said at a press conference on Friday night that no arrests had been made by the time, adding that investigators were working to learn the circumstances around the shooting.At the time of the shooting, Eden Prairie was playing Minnetonka as an announcer asked everyone present on the field and in the stands to evacuate the stadium.District officials urged people attending the game to either head to the baseball diamonds to exit or be picked up at Round Lake Park. No homecoming, in any community, should be disrupted by gun violence, Walz said, adding: Minnesotans are keeping students and families in our thoughts tonight. The Eden Prairie football team said that the game will resume on Saturday (October 3) at 11 am.

extraction.body: Parents at Eden Prairie High School say safety is still a top concern after a homecoming shooting outside the stadium. Weeks after two people were shot outside a game earlier this month, Eden Prairie High School had metal detectors, bag checks and a larger police presence at Friday night’s football game. The added security comes after a community meeting where parents raised concerns about gang activity and secure entrances in school buildings. “I think you look at metal detectors and all the security and you wonder if it’s overkill, but like I said, all it takes is one time,” Bryan Anderson, a parent of an Eden Prairie football player, said. Days earlier, parents also spoke at a community meeting about safety in the stadium and inside school buildings. A woman at the meeting said she was upset after the shooting. “I am not shocked, but I am angry, I have triplets at Eden Prairie.” she declared. David Barr, a Farmington parent, said he came to the game hoping school leaders and police were staying on top of security. “Just kind of not quite sure what the environment will be like. But you know, hopefully, they’re on top of it,” Barr said. 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS asked the district and Eden Prairie police whether there had been more security upgrades since that meeting, but both declined interview requests. Police also declined to share whether any further security changes had been made since the meeting. “As long as it keeps people safe, I’m fine with it. Don’t have any concerns. I would rather not have that then the alternative.” Barr said. Police said days after the Oct. 2 shooting outside the stadium, shots were fired at a gas station about a mile away. During that community meeting, the Eden Prairie Police Chief said officers are increasing patrols to stop park takeovers. The district said it will keep the added security measures in place into basketball season. “As long as they were patrolling the high school, that’s the main thing, to protect our children nowadays, because they shouldn’t have to see this.” Terry Dekarski, an Eden Prairie resident, said. Days earlier, parents also spoke at a community meeting about safety in the stadium and inside school buildings. A woman at the meeting said she was upset after the shooting. “I am not shocked, but I am angry, I have triplets at Eden Prairie.” she declared. David Barr, a Farmington parent, said he came to the game hoping school leaders and police were staying on top of security. “Just kind of not quite sure what the environment will be like. But you know, hopefully, they’re on top of it,” Barr said. 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS asked the district and Eden Prairie police whether there had been more security upgrades since that meeting, but both declined interview requests. Police also declined to share whether any further security changes had been made since the meeting. “As long as it keeps people safe, I’m fine with it. Don’t have any concerns. I would rather not have that then the alternative.” Barr said. Police said days after the Oct. 2 shooting outside the stadium, shots were fired at a gas station about a mile away. During that community meeting, the Eden Prairie Police Chief said officers are increasing patrols to stop park takeovers. The district said it will keep the added security measures in place into basketball season. “As long as they were patrolling the high school, that’s the main thing, to protect our children nowadays, because they shouldn’t have to see this.” Terry Dekarski, an Eden Prairie resident, said. passages: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.
