extraction.body: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange . A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. sources.title: Binance Hack: Why refunds alone won't solve crypto's security problem
passages: He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years.

Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach.

This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held.

This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks.

Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards.

The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes?

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion security breach at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has renewed concerns about the safety of digital assets and the risks of keeping investments on centralised trading platforms. While the exchange has pledged to cover all losses and around $3 billion worth of assets have reportedly been frozen, the incident raises a larger question: how can crypto platforms prevent such attacks rather than simply compensate investors after a breach?Binance's preliminary investigation has pointed to a possible compromise of a developer engineer's laptop, which may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service and initiate unauthorised withdrawals. The incident highlights the risks associated with internal access to systems handling large amounts of digital assets.Vineet Budki, Partner and CEO of Sigma Capital, believes the solution lies in stronger security measures, better industry cooperation and greater investor awareness.In an interview with CNBC-TV18, Budki said cyberattacks were not new to the digital world, but the growing use of online platforms for financial transactions had increased the potential consequences of a security breach. He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years. Web 3 has taken this further by allowing people to transact through digital platforms.This has increased the financial stakes involved in cyberattacks."Anything that involves a transaction carries the risk of being hacked," Budki said.He pointed to incidents such as the theft of $80 million from the Bank of Bangladesh in 2016 and the Mt. Gox and WazirX hacks to underline that security breaches are not unique to any one segment of the digital economy.The Binance incident also raises questions about the security of internal systems. If an employee's compromised device can provide access to services that authorise transactions, exchanges need to ensure that such access cannot be exploited to move large amounts of assets.According to Budki, technology will continue to improve, but attackers will also find new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held. Investors should consider their overall exposure to crypto alongside investments in real estate, gold and other assets.He also advised against keeping all cryptocurrency holdings on one trading platform. Instead, investors should consider splitting their holdings between exchanges and private wallets.This brings self-custody into focus. Unlike assets held on an exchange, cryptocurrency stored in a private wallet gives investors greater control over how their holdings are accessed and transferred."Not your wallet, not your money," Budki said.His point is that investors who leave their assets on an exchange depend on the platform's security systems and controls. Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach. While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources. However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards. This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks. Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock. The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes? Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution. Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency. Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen. Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources.

However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards.

This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks.

Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock.

The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes?
Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution.

Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency.

Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen.

Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

extraction.body: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange . A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure.
There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore.

Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.

"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this."
Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.

A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.

In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note.

"They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today."

Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
"Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack.

Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents.

However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach.

It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure.
"I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said.

"Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added.

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion security breach at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has renewed concerns about the safety of digital assets and the risks of keeping investments on centralised trading platforms. While the exchange has pledged to cover all losses and around $3 billion worth of assets have reportedly been frozen, the incident raises a larger question: how can crypto platforms prevent such attacks rather than simply compensate investors after a breach?Binance's preliminary investigation has pointed to a possible compromise of a developer engineer's laptop, which may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service and initiate unauthorised withdrawals. The incident highlights the risks associated with internal access to systems handling large amounts of digital assets.Vineet Budki, Partner and CEO of Sigma Capital, believes the solution lies in stronger security measures, better industry cooperation and greater investor awareness.In an interview with CNBC-TV18, Budki said cyberattacks were not new to the digital world, but the growing use of online platforms for financial transactions had increased the potential consequences of a security breach. He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years. Web 3 has taken this further by allowing people to transact through digital platforms.This has increased the financial stakes involved in cyberattacks."Anything that involves a transaction carries the risk of being hacked," Budki said.He pointed to incidents such as the theft of $80 million from the Bank of Bangladesh in 2016 and the Mt. Gox and WazirX hacks to underline that security breaches are not unique to any one segment of the digital economy.The Binance incident also raises questions about the security of internal systems. If an employee's compromised device can provide access to services that authorise transactions, exchanges need to ensure that such access cannot be exploited to move large amounts of assets.According to Budki, technology will continue to improve, but attackers will also find new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held. Investors should consider their overall exposure to crypto alongside investments in real estate, gold and other assets.He also advised against keeping all cryptocurrency holdings on one trading platform. Instead, investors should consider splitting their holdings between exchanges and private wallets.This brings self-custody into focus. Unlike assets held on an exchange, cryptocurrency stored in a private wallet gives investors greater control over how their holdings are accessed and transferred."Not your wallet, not your money," Budki said.His point is that investors who leave their assets on an exchange depend on the platform's security systems and controls. Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach. While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources. However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards. This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks. Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock. The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes? Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution. Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency. Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen. Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

29, with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets.
About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update.
Blockchain investigators at TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea , but neither the U.S. government or Binance has publicly confirmed any source for the hack.
Tanguma said keeping coins offline can protect against the kind of attack that hit Binance, though there are other risks associated with this digital security approach.

The attackers manipulated the system that approves withdrawals, the same approach used in last year's $1.5 billion theft from Bybit, which targeted a transfer out of cold storage," Tanguma said, noting that every custody setup has a weak point, and in most of them it is a single one.

By comparison, Binance's emergency reserve, the Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, is estimated at roughly $1 billion to $1.2 billion, and excluding the funds that were frozen, this represented about one-third of the loss.
The company said it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds and already held more than $5 billion in corresponding token assets.

extraction.body: For generations, most Americans have deposited their money in banks knowing that if somehow things went sideways, their funds would be covered by the full force of the government's treasury. Up to $250,000 in losses are covered through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), born out of the ashes of the Great Depression. Crypto investors are probably wishing for an FDIC equivalent after Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was hacked on Oct. 29, with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update. The Securities and Exchange Commission's research from 2024 and 2025 puts that figure closer to 15%, and estimated that roughly 9% of the investing public owned crypto at the time of its survey. Its survey work indicates cryptocurrency ownership is more common for younger individuals, men, and those with higher risk tolerance, but also possessing higher financial literacy. Many exchanges say customers will be paid back if something goes wrong. Josephine Wolff, professor of cybersecurity policy at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, said there "really aren't any legal protections for crypto assets equivalent to FDIC insurance." Customers could try to sue a hacked exchange, she said, for instance by claiming it was negligent, or may recover some funds if the exchange declares bankruptcy, as happened with FTX. But "there's no guarantee of compensation," she said. Michael Tanguma, co-founder and CEO of Onramp Bitcoin, a bitcoin financial services and custody firm, said that when an exchange is hacked, customers are usually repaid, "but only because the exchange decides to pay and has the money to do so." "Nothing in the law requires it to," Tanguma said. "Some stolen funds can be frozen. Tether and Circle, the companies behind the two largest dollar-backed tokens, froze billions of dollars of this week's stolen money, and law enforcement occasionally recovers assets years later," Tanguma said. But he added that bitcoin has no company behind it that can freeze it, so once it leaves your control, it is almost always gone. Customers who lose funds individually are in a very different situation than those caught up in an exchange attack. "When your own account is compromised, through a stolen password, a phishing link, or a hijacked phone number, the outlook is much worse," Tanguma said, noting that exchanges generally treat those losses as the customer's problem, and because crypto transactions are final once confirmed, there is no bank to call and no charge to dispute. "The stolen funds came from wallets the exchange keeps connected to the internet to process everyday withdrawals, not from its offline reserves," Tanguma said. "On an exchange, that point is the company: its employees, its approval systems, its finances, and its willingness to repay you," Tanguma said. When you hold your own coins, he said, that point is you: a lost device, a backup found by the wrong person, a tampered device bought from an unofficial seller, a transaction approved under pressure, or a family unable to reach the funds after a death. Once a transfer confirms, there's no chargeback and no one who can reverse it," Reck said. And there's of course also speculation. passages: For generations, most Americans have deposited their money in banks knowing that if somehow things went sideways, their funds would be covered by the full force of the government's treasury. Up to $250,000 in losses are covered through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), born out of the ashes of the Great Depression.

Crypto investors are probably wishing for an FDIC equivalent after Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was hacked on Oct. 29, with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update.

In a security update on Saturday, the exchange said it had replenished 90% of stolen assets and was committed to covering the remaining 10%. Blockchain investigators at TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea , but neither the U.S. government or Binance has publicly confirmed any source for the hack.
Understanding how crypto is protected online and what mechanisms exist to serve a role similar to insurance is increasingly important as more Americans invest in cryptocurrency.

Roughly one in five U.S. adults say they have invested in, traded, or used crypto , according to Pew Research Center, a figure that is even higher among upper income households (27%). The Securities and Exchange Commission's research from 2024 and 2025 puts that figure closer to 15%, and estimated that roughly 9% of the investing public owned crypto at the time of its survey. Its survey work indicates cryptocurrency ownership is more common for younger individuals, men, and those with higher risk tolerance, but also possessing higher financial literacy.

While Binance was making good on its pledge in the aftermath of the hack to cover all losses with its SAFU (Secure Asset Fund for Users) and other company's funds — and that there's no evidence of a wallet private-key leak in this incident — Nikolas Behar, a cybersecurity expert and professor at the University of San Diego, said crypto investors need to understand when using crypto platforms that a pledge is just a pledge "until there's an actual payout."

If something happens to your crypto, most consumers are left to navigate a patchwork of options that vary from exchange to exchange and are often very ambiguous. Many exchanges say customers will be paid back if something goes wrong.
Josephine Wolff, professor of cybersecurity policy at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, said there "really aren't any legal protections for crypto assets equivalent to FDIC insurance."

Customers could try to sue a hacked exchange, she said, for instance by claiming it was negligent, or may recover some funds if the exchange declares bankruptcy, as happened with FTX. But "there's no guarantee of compensation," she said.

Michael Tanguma, co-founder and CEO of Onramp Bitcoin, a bitcoin financial services and custody firm, said that when an exchange is hacked, customers are usually repaid, "but only because the exchange decides to pay and has the money to do so."
"Nothing in the law requires it to," Tanguma said.

"Some stolen funds can be frozen. Tether and Circle, the companies behind the two largest dollar-backed tokens, froze billions of dollars of this week's stolen money, and law enforcement occasionally recovers assets years later," Tanguma said. But he added that bitcoin has no company behind it that can freeze it, so once it leaves your control, it is almost always gone.
Customers who lose funds individually are in a very different situation than those caught up in an exchange attack.

"When your own account is compromised, through a stolen password, a phishing link, or a hijacked phone number, the outlook is much worse," Tanguma said, noting that exchanges generally treat those losses as the customer's problem, and because crypto transactions are final once confirmed, there is no bank to call and no charge to dispute.
Tanguma said keeping coins offline can protect against the kind of attack that hit Binance, though there are other risks associated with this digital security approach.

"The stolen funds came from wallets the exchange keeps connected to the internet to process everyday withdrawals, not from its offline reserves," Tanguma said. But he added that the details of this hack point to a larger problem.

"Binance says no keys were leaked. The attackers manipulated the system that approves withdrawals, the same approach used in last year's $1.5 billion theft from Bybit, which targeted a transfer out of cold storage," Tanguma said, noting that every custody setup has a weak point, and in most of them it is a single one.

"On an exchange, that point is the company: its employees, its approval systems, its finances, and its willingness to repay you," Tanguma said. When you hold your own coins, he said, that point is you: a lost device, a backup found by the wrong person, a tampered device bought from an unofficial seller, a transaction approved under pressure, or a family unable to reach the funds after a death.
"Moving savings off an exchange trades one kind of risk for another. It does not remove risk," Tanguma said.

Bitget, another major exchange, had to tap an in-house fund to reimburse customers after a $388 million hack in September. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said its User Protection Fund, which held more than $464 million, covered the loss. extraction.body: The largest group of single-issue super PACs in United States history is pouring millions of dollars into congressional races across the country. Cryptocurrency groups outpaced online betting and data center development groups in federal corporate political spending this election cycle, according to Public Citizen . Crypto-tied organizations have contributed more than $200 million in this election cycle. The industry is hoping to repeat the success of 2024, when super PACs spent $250 million to elect pro-crypto lawmakers and reshape Congress. Crypto juggernaut Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs are throwing their support behind 33 House candidates — 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats — seen as key supporters of the industry's priorities. The network is prioritizing six House incumbents by injecting a baseline of $1 million into their campaigns. Republicans Bryan Steil of Wisconsin , who chairs a digital assets subcommittee in the lower chamber, as well as French Hill of Arkansas and Bill Huizenga of Michigan , who serve as the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, respectively. Democratic lawmakers receiving at least $1 million from Fairshake include Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon; Derek Tran of California; and Steven Horsford of Nevada . Fairshake's spending spree has been supercharged by digital asset-focused companies, like cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global. Coinbase established itself as one of the largest corporate political donors in modern history in the 2024 election cycle, contributing $79 million to federal races, according to OpenSecrets . That included a $1 million dollar personal contribution from CEO Brian Armstrong to Fairshake in 2023. Coinbase donated $25 million to Fairshake's midterm efforts in 2025, according to the super PAC. "The ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century," Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, told CNBC. "In an era where affordability is top of mind for American voters, it's important that we find a way that we can move money more cheaply, that we can invest more easily, and that we can transact more quickly, and fundamentally that is not something that Democrats or Republicans should oppose," he said. The industry faced pushback in the current Congress as it urged lawmakers to pass landmark crypto legislation. In September, the Clarity Act, a bipartisan set of market structure rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate after Democrats argued it didn't do enough to prevent top government officials from profiting off crypto ventures. The stalemate over ethics comes as Americans grow increasingly gloomy toward government corruption. A Gallup poll released in September found a record 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread. Changing voter priorities also present a headwind for crypto's legislative efforts. The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey this month found only 20% of respondents rate the economy as excellent or good, down from 27% in July. "Overwhelmingly, the issue right now is the affordability crisis," said Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), one of the three Democratic candidates Fairshake is giving more than $1 million. Horsford, who introduced bipartisan legislation in May to modernize federal tax laws for digital assets, said crypto is still on the minds of some voters, alongside economic uncertainty. "It definitely comes up in town halls and community meetings, in forums that I have, especially with small businesses who are looking to use digital assets and bitcoin," said Horsford. "They're being asked more and more by their consumers whether or not they take those those payments for services and goods." November's elections will test crypto's continued influence on Washington. The crypto industry is laser-focused on the Ohio Senate race between Democratic nominee, and former Senator, Sherrod Brown , a longtime crypto critic, and Republican Jon Husted, who is pro-crypto and currently holds the seat. Fairshake spent about $40 million to unseat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill. The super PAC this cycle told CNBC it has already spent $55 million to oppose Brown. A Marist poll conducted Oct. 15-18 showed Brown holding a four-point edge over Husted among likely voters statewide, within the margin of error of 4.5%. "A lot of these races are going to be extremely tight," said Mason Lynaugh, executive director of the advocacy group Stand With Crypto, launched by Coinbase in 2023. This election cycle, Stand With Crypto has endorsed a total of 45 candidates, 42 in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate. "We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added. Digital assets and infrastructure company Ripple spent a total of $63.65 million in federal contributions last election, according to OpenSecrets , and the company is spending millions again now. Ripple donated $25 million in 2025, according to Fairshake. Asked if the crypto industry got a good return on its investment, Stu Alderoty, Ripple's chief legal officer, told CNBC, "I think compared to where the industry was two years ago to where the industry is today, yes, I would say that that is a very good return." Alderoty pointed to the GENIUS Act, which established the first federal framework for dollar-pegged stablecoins. President Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, the first-ever standalone crypto legislation in the United States. But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing. Former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, now a board member of the crypto exchange OKX, told CNBC that lawmaking is unlikely if Congress changes hands in January. "You're going to have a Democratic Congress overseeing an administration, the Trump administration, where the regulators are making decisions under the scrutiny of a hostile Congress, and that is not a good place to be because the Congress will be at loggerheads with the administration," he said. Horsford, the Nevada congressman, told CNBC that time is of the essence. If the Clarity Act doesn't advance before the end of the year, Congress will have to start from scratch on a new market structure bill for digital assets. And crypto super PACs are hoping their spending still has the influence to shape which lawmakers work on the next round of legislation. "Regardless of who is elected in Congress, we're going to continue to see more regulatory clarity in this space," Coinbase's VanGrack, a former SEC senior advisor, told CNBC. "It may be an open question whether we get all the way across the goal line, but it's not an open question about whether we're going to have progress and continue to see progress in terms of regulatory clarity in crypto," VanGrack added. "We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added.

But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing.

extraction.body: The largest group of single-issue super PACs in United States history is pouring millions of dollars into congressional races across the country. Cryptocurrency groups outpaced online betting and data center development groups in federal corporate political spending this election cycle, according to Public Citizen . Crypto-tied organizations have contributed more than $200 million in this election cycle. The industry is hoping to repeat the success of 2024, when super PACs spent $250 million to elect pro-crypto lawmakers and reshape Congress. Crypto juggernaut Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs are throwing their support behind 33 House candidates — 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats — seen as key supporters of the industry's priorities. The network is prioritizing six House incumbents by injecting a baseline of $1 million into their campaigns. Republicans Bryan Steil of Wisconsin , who chairs a digital assets subcommittee in the lower chamber, as well as French Hill of Arkansas and Bill Huizenga of Michigan , who serve as the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, respectively. Democratic lawmakers receiving at least $1 million from Fairshake include Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon; Derek Tran of California; and Steven Horsford of Nevada . Fairshake's spending spree has been supercharged by digital asset-focused companies, like cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global. Coinbase established itself as one of the largest corporate political donors in modern history in the 2024 election cycle, contributing $79 million to federal races, according to OpenSecrets . That included a $1 million dollar personal contribution from CEO Brian Armstrong to Fairshake in 2023. Coinbase donated $25 million to Fairshake's midterm efforts in 2025, according to the super PAC. "The ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century," Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, told CNBC. "In an era where affordability is top of mind for American voters, it's important that we find a way that we can move money more cheaply, that we can invest more easily, and that we can transact more quickly, and fundamentally that is not something that Democrats or Republicans should oppose," he said. The industry faced pushback in the current Congress as it urged lawmakers to pass landmark crypto legislation. In September, the Clarity Act, a bipartisan set of market structure rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate after Democrats argued it didn't do enough to prevent top government officials from profiting off crypto ventures. The stalemate over ethics comes as Americans grow increasingly gloomy toward government corruption. A Gallup poll released in September found a record 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread. Changing voter priorities also present a headwind for crypto's legislative efforts. The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey this month found only 20% of respondents rate the economy as excellent or good, down from 27% in July. "Overwhelmingly, the issue right now is the affordability crisis," said Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), one of the three Democratic candidates Fairshake is giving more than $1 million. Horsford, who introduced bipartisan legislation in May to modernize federal tax laws for digital assets, said crypto is still on the minds of some voters, alongside economic uncertainty. "It definitely comes up in town halls and community meetings, in forums that I have, especially with small businesses who are looking to use digital assets and bitcoin," said Horsford. "They're being asked more and more by their consumers whether or not they take those those payments for services and goods." November's elections will test crypto's continued influence on Washington. The crypto industry is laser-focused on the Ohio Senate race between Democratic nominee, and former Senator, Sherrod Brown , a longtime crypto critic, and Republican Jon Husted, who is pro-crypto and currently holds the seat. Fairshake spent about $40 million to unseat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill. The super PAC this cycle told CNBC it has already spent $55 million to oppose Brown. A Marist poll conducted Oct. 15-18 showed Brown holding a four-point edge over Husted among likely voters statewide, within the margin of error of 4.5%. "A lot of these races are going to be extremely tight," said Mason Lynaugh, executive director of the advocacy group Stand With Crypto, launched by Coinbase in 2023. This election cycle, Stand With Crypto has endorsed a total of 45 candidates, 42 in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate. "We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added. Digital assets and infrastructure company Ripple spent a total of $63.65 million in federal contributions last election, according to OpenSecrets , and the company is spending millions again now. Ripple donated $25 million in 2025, according to Fairshake. Asked if the crypto industry got a good return on its investment, Stu Alderoty, Ripple's chief legal officer, told CNBC, "I think compared to where the industry was two years ago to where the industry is today, yes, I would say that that is a very good return." Alderoty pointed to the GENIUS Act, which established the first federal framework for dollar-pegged stablecoins. President Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, the first-ever standalone crypto legislation in the United States. But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing. Former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, now a board member of the crypto exchange OKX, told CNBC that lawmaking is unlikely if Congress changes hands in January. "You're going to have a Democratic Congress overseeing an administration, the Trump administration, where the regulators are making decisions under the scrutiny of a hostile Congress, and that is not a good place to be because the Congress will be at loggerheads with the administration," he said. Horsford, the Nevada congressman, told CNBC that time is of the essence. If the Clarity Act doesn't advance before the end of the year, Congress will have to start from scratch on a new market structure bill for digital assets. And crypto super PACs are hoping their spending still has the influence to shape which lawmakers work on the next round of legislation. "Regardless of who is elected in Congress, we're going to continue to see more regulatory clarity in this space," Coinbase's VanGrack, a former SEC senior advisor, told CNBC. "It may be an open question whether we get all the way across the goal line, but it's not an open question about whether we're going to have progress and continue to see progress in terms of regulatory clarity in crypto," VanGrack added. sources.title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety - CNBC
passages: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

extraction.body: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange . A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. extraction.body: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange . A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. extraction.body: Vic Mensa is one of those people who has done so many things that it’s hard to remember where you were first introduced to him. Or maybe his house-influenced single “Down On My Luck”? Maybe you didn’t even realize that Mensa was a rapper. Or perhaps you’re mostly aware of him through his activism, social media presence (peeling oranges and waxing poetic), or his podcast The Vic Mensa Show. Part of the secret to being so prolific, it turns out, is Voice Memos. Songs, essay ideas, orange tree thoughts, voice notes to myself at some wild hour, little things my son says that I do not want to lose. My phone is a million distractions in one rectangle, but Voice Memos is one of the few parts of it that still feels honest. That’s definitely where my voice has really found its legs. I started out peeling an orange and talking through whatever was on my mind, and it turned into this whole conversation with people about politics, history, music, grief, jokes, fatherhood, all of it. That response helped show me there was room for The Vic Mensa Show too. What is the last GIF or meme you used? [Image: Ummm… that is not Vic Mensa.

passages: Quarterly earnings reports from hyperscalers this week spooked investors.
Alphabet saw its cash flow sink deeper into negative territory in the third quarter, with the Google parent also joining Meta and Amazon in charging ahead with massive spending plans.
On Thursday, Alphabet fell about 12%, its worst day on record.
The funding round was also upstaged by Anthropic, according to the report, as OpenAI's arch-rival prepares to go public next month.
Meanwhile, S&P sees Meta's capex reaching $140 billion this year, topping $225 billion in 2027, hitting $252 billion in 2028, and then flattening out from there.
At the same time, OpenAI was seeking more capital just as other AI giants tapped financial markets heavily.
This past week alone, Elon Musk said SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing, Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity, and Microsoft raised $25 billion in a bond sale.
Following a brutal selloff in tech stocks over the past week, OpenAI slashed the target on its latest fundraising round to $20 billion from $30 billion, sources told the Financial Times .
That also cut its expected valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion.

The prospect of hyperscalers continuing to hemorrhage funds was too much for S&P Global, which cut its outlook on Meta to "negative" from "stable" late Friday, citing negative cash flow and uncertainty around capital expenditure ​plans.
The credit ratings agency maintained Meta at AA- but warned ⁠the social media leader's leverage could top 1.0x as soon as 2027, which is the downgrade threshold for the current rating.
That's up from about 0.1x in 2025 and primarily reflects its strategy of leasing data center capacity rather than from its debt issuance.

The bearish environment on Wall Street also comes as rising bond yields have sent borrowing costs sharply higher, the political backlash against data centers is expected to help Democrats retake Congress, and the Iran war could re-escalate after midterm elections.

Microsoft reported strong cloud growth and stayed cash flow positive, though it said its capital spending will accelerate, while AI chip maker SK Hynix blew away earnings forecasts.

In a statement to Fortune , a Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with S&P's assessment of its AI monetization capabilities, pointing to "significant product and business opportunities" ahead.
"Meta is already delivering stronger engagement, better recommendations, and greater returns for businesses as a result of AI investments," the spokesperson continued.

"We believe the technology and infrastructure we're building now will open new revenue streams, create long-term shareholder value, and bring us closer to delivering personal superintelligence to everyone."
Meta's rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added.
OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
