The seemingly endless gusher of capital that's been showered on Silicon Valley during the AI boom may be coming to an end soon as Wall Street pushes back on massive spending plans. Following a brutal selloff in tech stocks over the past week, OpenAI slashed the target on its latest fundraising round to $20 billion from $30 billion, sources told the Financial Times . That also cut its expected valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion. The funding round was also upstaged by Anthropic, according to the report, as OpenAI's arch-rival prepares to go public next month. Ahead of its IPO, Anthropic filed an S-1 on Monday that showed revenue has soared and its cash flow turned positive in the first half of this year. OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The timing couldn't have been worse. Quarterly earnings reports from hyperscalers this week spooked investors. Alphabet saw its cash flow sink deeper into negative territory in the third quarter, with the Google parent also joining Meta and Amazon in charging ahead with massive spending plans. On Thursday, Alphabet fell about 12%, its worst day on record. To be sure, there were other positive signs as well, in addition to Anthropic's bullish S-1. Microsoft reported strong cloud growth and stayed cash flow positive, though it said its capital spending will accelerate, while AI chip maker SK Hynix blew away earnings forecasts. But the narrative had already turned bearish, especially after AI debt fears sent shares and bonds of "neocloud" companies tumbling earlier this month. At the same time, OpenAI was seeking more capital just as other AI giants tapped financial markets heavily. This past week alone, Elon Musk said SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing, Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity, and Microsoft raised $25 billion in a bond sale. The prospect of hyperscalers continuing to hemorrhage funds was too much for S&P Global, which cut its outlook on Meta to "negative" from "stable" late Friday, citing negative cash flow and uncertainty around capital expenditure ​plans. The credit ratings agency maintained Meta at AA- but warned ⁠the social media leader's leverage could top 1.0x as soon as 2027, which is the downgrade threshold for the current rating. That's up from about 0.1x in 2025 and primarily reflects its strategy of leasing data center capacity rather than from its debt issuance. Meanwhile, S&P sees Meta's capex reaching $140 billion this year, topping $225 billion in 2027, hitting $252 billion in 2028, and then flattening out from there. As a result, it expects free operating cash flow to remain negative: -$22 billion this year, -$71 billion in 2027, and -$39 billion in 2028. Of course, other hyperscalers are spending heavily and running cash deficits, but S&P also said Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers. "While we believe the company intends to monetize these investments via improved advertising tools that support faster ad revenue growth, as well as from the development of new revenue streams stemming from its introduction of agentic apps such as Muse, it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years," S&P said. Meta's rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added. In a statement to Fortune , a Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with S&P's assessment of its AI monetization capabilities, pointing to "significant product and business opportunities" ahead. "Meta is already delivering stronger engagement, better recommendations, and greater returns for businesses as a result of AI investments," the spokesperson continued. "We believe the technology and infrastructure we're building now will open new revenue streams, create long-term shareholder value, and bring us closer to delivering personal superintelligence to everyone." The bearish environment on Wall Street also comes as rising bond yields have sent borrowing costs sharply higher, the political backlash against data centers is expected to help Democrats retake Congress, and the Iran war could re-escalate after midterm elections. Still, some bullish voices aren't convinced the AI boom is about to go bust, and even think some retrenchment is a good thing . According to market veteran Ed Yardeni, the AI investment boom faces financial, physical, and political constraints. If any of these constraints worsen, stocks could dive further, especially considering that AI is now a major driver of corporate earnings and GDP growth, he said in a note this week. "However, we view these constraints as healthy for the durability of the AI boom!" he added. For example, if the supply of capital doesn't flow as easily, it could lead to more efficient allocation, lowering the risk of overinvestment. Yardeni expects hyperscalers to retain access to financing—thanks to their strong balance sheets—and keep spending. In his view, it all comes down to the U.S. economy, which he said has performed remarkably well over the past few decades. Even the midterm elections are unlikely to derail it, regardless of which party controls Congress. "Further AI jitters therefore could set up buying opportunities rather than signal the end of the boom," he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

sources.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

extraction.body: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. You can contact or verify outreach from Rebecca by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at rebeccabellan.491 on Signal.

Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week.

Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank .

It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.
Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.

These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

sources.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow - The Business Times
passages: The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

But now there is growing uncertainty around just how easily more money can be obtained – and how much of it will be paid back. Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave. Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations. Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s. At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI. The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive AI projects. The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out. Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines. The spread, or extra premium that investors demand to put their money into risky AI debt investments, has shot up more than 50 per cent over the past six months, according to Barclays, the investment bank. “The market is on a knife’s edge everywhere,” said Alexandra Coleman, founder of Azraq, a data centre risk researcher. A lot is riding on the continuation of the borrowing binge. Every week lately, economists, banks and private equity firms project higher and higher amounts of debt that they say will be needed to finance the AI systems that their boosters assert will run the world in a few years. Virtually every major mutual fund company, insurer and private equity firm has been buying up the AI debt, to say nothing of the scores of individual investors who have poured money into skyrocketing AI companies. Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future. Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire. A CoreWeave spokesperson, Lia Davis, said the company disagreed with the WeWork comparison. “The complexity of our financing reflects discipline, which is a point of pride for us,” she said in a statement. Another worry is the growing number of US data-centre projects being delayed by permitting issues or, in some cases, falling through. Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects. Aterio, a data centre researcher, said it was looking less likely that Project Lighthouse’s four data centres would start operating before 2029. That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due. At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000. Some investors see a potential silver lining to the troubles. sources.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

extraction.body: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. sources.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow - The Business Times
passages: The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.

facts.text: Quarterly earnings reports from hyperscalers this week spooked investors.
Alphabet saw its cash flow sink deeper into negative territory in the third quarter, with the Google parent also joining Meta and Amazon in charging ahead with massive spending plans.
On Thursday, Alphabet fell about 12%, its worst day on record.
The funding round was also upstaged by Anthropic, according to the report, as OpenAI's arch-rival prepares to go public next month.
Meanwhile, S&P sees Meta's capex reaching $140 billion this year, topping $225 billion in 2027, hitting $252 billion in 2028, and then flattening out from there.
At the same time, OpenAI was seeking more capital just as other AI giants tapped financial markets heavily.
This past week alone, Elon Musk said SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing, Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity, and Microsoft raised $25 billion in a bond sale.
Following a brutal selloff in tech stocks over the past week, OpenAI slashed the target on its latest fundraising round to $20 billion from $30 billion, sources told the Financial Times .
That also cut its expected valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion.

The prospect of hyperscalers continuing to hemorrhage funds was too much for S&P Global, which cut its outlook on Meta to "negative" from "stable" late Friday, citing negative cash flow and uncertainty around capital expenditure ​plans.
The credit ratings agency maintained Meta at AA- but warned ⁠the social media leader's leverage could top 1.0x as soon as 2027, which is the downgrade threshold for the current rating.
That's up from about 0.1x in 2025 and primarily reflects its strategy of leasing data center capacity rather than from its debt issuance.

The bearish environment on Wall Street also comes as rising bond yields have sent borrowing costs sharply higher, the political backlash against data centers is expected to help Democrats retake Congress, and the Iran war could re-escalate after midterm elections.

"Meta is already delivering stronger engagement, better recommendations, and greater returns for businesses as a result of AI investments," the spokesperson continued.

"We believe the technology and infrastructure we're building now will open new revenue streams, create long-term shareholder value, and bring us closer to delivering personal superintelligence to everyone."
Meta's rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added.
OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets. Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars. Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003 . “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic. Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist. TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis. An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report. Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets. The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who was jailed for four months in 2024 after pleading guilty to money laundering violations. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025. The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.” Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks. Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”. In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.” Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. “It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong. North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic. Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the FBI and the US Secret Service. Tether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m. The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers. Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system. Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident. The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. However, it is understood there are no active concerns. The Bank declined to comment.

sources.title: $6.3 billion Binance hack is largest crypto theft on record - CNBC
passages: Binance said Friday that a security incident impacted about $6.3 billion in client assets, with around $3 billion frozen on-chain, marking the largest crypto hack on record.
In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack.
Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.

The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.

This week's breach "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Michael Selig, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said Friday in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview.
5 proposed a framework that would effectively put crypto exchanges under federal government oversight — after Congress failed to approve legislation to regulate the asset.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said in a post.
Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls.
It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.
"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.
We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said.
Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,187.60 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets.
Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said.
The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected.
The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group , Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.

The company later added it began recovering assets impacted by the breach after pledging to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, which the company created in 2018 as a protection for clients in the event of a hack. It wasn't clear how the attack took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions. The FBI said Friday it was aware of the incident and was in touch with "relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate ​potential impacts, ​and ⁠coordinate appropriate investigative steps." It wasn't clear either who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits . "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said in a post. Blockchain data platform Chainalysis also said this appears "be the work of North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor . This group has repeatedly targeted the cryptocurrency industry, exchanges, DeFi protocols, and investors, to raise funds for the regime. We base our intelligence assessment on on-chain activity observed in the hours following the hack." Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said. The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected. Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls. It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours. "We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said. The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group , Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack. Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges. This week's breach "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Michael Selig, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said Friday in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview. The U.S. derivatives regulator on Oct. 5 proposed a framework that would effectively put crypto exchanges under federal government oversight — after Congress failed to approve legislation to regulate the asset. "The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States. We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cyber security safeguards that we have in our markets today," he said. Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,187.60 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets. Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, experienced a record $6.3 billion security exploit this week Dan Kitwood / Getty Images Crypto exchange Binance said Saturday it has been able to replace 90% of the amount stolen after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform that the FBI blamed on North Korea. Binance said it was able to replace the funds taken in the record hack by using company money to buy new tokens. The remaining 10% consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. Crypto prices fell Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe. The FBI on Saturday said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Members of the unit were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology. Teng said Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals Sunday. Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X. Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT Saturday, as part of its proof-of-reserves process. Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum ratio of 1:1 once the full proof was available, it said.

Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.
North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered.
The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.
Q&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?
“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.

extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, experienced a record $6.3 billion security exploit this week Dan Kitwood / Getty Images Crypto exchange Binance said Saturday it has been able to replace 90% of the amount stolen after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform that the FBI blamed on North Korea. Binance said it was able to replace the funds taken in the record hack by using company money to buy new tokens. The remaining 10% consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. Crypto prices fell Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe. The FBI on Saturday said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Members of the unit were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology. Teng said Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals Sunday. Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X. Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT Saturday, as part of its proof-of-reserves process. Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum ratio of 1:1 once the full proof was available, it said.

“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.

The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group , Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.

A federal judge in Mississippi has rejected an effort by the Trump administration to shut down a lawsuit brought by the NAACP against Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, allowing a closely watched environmental justice case to continue. The lawsuit, filed by the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of operating a gas-fired power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, without the environmental permits required under the Clean Air Act. The plant supplies power to xAI’s massive Colossus 2 data center, which supports the company’s artificial intelligence operations. The case has drawn attention because of the plant’s location near predominantly Black communities in North Mississippi and South Memphis. Reuters previously reported that pollution tied to the project has raised concerns about whether the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is placing disproportionate environmental burdens on Black neighborhoods. The Trump administration, acting through the Environmental Protection Agency, sought to intervene in the case and argued that the EPA had the authority to terminate the lawsuit. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown disagreed with that position Monday. Brown ruled that the EPA could participate in the case, but said nothing in the Clean Air Act gives the agency the power to unilaterally dismiss a citizen lawsuit simply because it has intervened. The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved. The lawsuit was originally filed in April. At the time, the NAACP accused xAI of operating dozens of methane gas turbines without the required permits, effectively creating a private power plant to meet the enormous energy demands of its data center. The organization has argued that nearby residents should not have to bear the health and environmental costs of the company’s rapid expansion. The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution. The organization is being represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice. The legal fight comes as communities across the country begin confronting the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, and developers are increasingly turning to on-site power generation to meet demand. That growth has prompted new questions about air quality, energy use and how quickly environmental regulations can keep pace with the AI boom. For the NAACP, the case is about more than one data center. It is part of a broader argument that Black communities should not be expected to absorb additional pollution in the name of technological progress, particularly when those communities have historically faced disproportionate exposure to industrial development and poor air quality. The judge’s ruling does not determine whether xAI violated environmental law. That question still has to be resolved in court. What it does mean is that the NAACP will be allowed to continue pressing its case.

The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved.

The lawsuit was originally filed in April. At the time, the NAACP accused xAI of operating dozens of methane gas turbines without the required permits, effectively creating a private power plant to meet the enormous energy demands of its data center. The organization has argued that nearby residents should not have to bear the health and environmental costs of the company’s rapid expansion.

The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution. The organization is being represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice.

The legal fight comes as communities across the country begin confronting the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, and developers are increasingly turning to on-site power generation to meet demand. That growth has prompted new questions about air quality, energy use and how quickly environmental regulations can keep pace with the AI boom.
For the NAACP, the case is about more than one data center.

It is part of a broader argument that Black communities should not be expected to absorb additional pollution in the name of technological progress, particularly when those communities have historically faced disproportionate exposure to industrial development and poor air quality.
The judge’s ruling does not determine whether xAI violated environmental law. That question still has to be resolved in court.
What it does mean is that the NAACP will be allowed to continue pressing its case.

extraction.body: A federal judge just handed the NAACP a major victory in its fight against xAI, allowing a lawsuit alleging Clean Air Act violations at the company's data center to move forward. With AI data centers consuming unprecedented amounts of energy and requiring extensive cooling systems, the ruling could reshape how tech companies approach regulatory compliance. The legal battle puts xAI, Elon Musk's artificial intelligence venture, squarely in the crosshairs of environmental justice advocates who argue the company's data center operations violate federal clean air standards. The judge's decision to let the case proceed past preliminary motions means xAI will now face discovery and potentially a trial on the merits of the NAACP's claims. Just last week, SpaceX closed a massive $40 billion debt deal to purchase GPUs for AI infrastructure, underscoring the breakneck pace of expansion across Musk's technology empire. That infrastructure buildout requires enormous data centers with corresponding energy demands and environmental footprints. The NAACP's lawsuit centers on allegations that xAI's data center operations produce air pollution that exceeds Clean Air Act thresholds without proper permitting or mitigation measures. Environmental advocates have increasingly raised concerns about the energy intensity of AI model training and inference, which requires thousands of high-powered chips running continuously in facilities that generate substantial heat and emissions. Data centers have become flashpoints in communities across the country as residents push back against facilities they see as bringing pollution, noise, and strain on local power grids without commensurate benefits. The judge's ruling doesn't determine the merits of the NAACP's claims, but it does mean the organization cleared the initial hurdles to proceed with litigation. That's significant because tech companies often succeed in getting environmental lawsuits dismissed on procedural grounds before reaching the substance of the allegations. For xAI, the lawsuit adds regulatory uncertainty at a crucial moment. The company competes with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta in the race to build more powerful AI systems, a competition that requires massive infrastructure investments. Companies have announced plans for dozens of new data centers to support AI workloads, often in regions offering tax incentives or cheap power. Legal experts say the case could establish important precedents about what level of environmental review and permitting AI data centers require. The Clean Air Act includes provisions for reviewing major new sources of pollution and protecting communities disproportionately affected by environmental hazards, both potentially relevant to large-scale AI infrastructure. The lawsuit also highlights tensions within Musk's broader business empire. The company's rapid growth has occasionally outpaced its ability to navigate complex regulatory frameworks. The case now moves into discovery, where the NAACP will have the opportunity to gather evidence about xAI's operations, emissions, and compliance with air quality standards. That process could reveal new details about how the company manages the environmental impacts of its data center operations and whether it obtained necessary permits before beginning operations. For the NAACP, the ruling represents validation of its strategy to use environmental law as a tool for protecting communities from the potential harms of AI infrastructure expansion. The organization has increasingly focused on technology policy issues, recognizing that decisions about where to locate data centers and other facilities have significant equity implications. The judge's decision to let this lawsuit proceed signals that AI companies can't assume their infrastructure expansion will face only technical and financial hurdles. As xAI and its rivals pour billions into data centers, they'll need to navigate not just the engineering challenges of training massive models, but also the regulatory and legal frameworks designed to protect air quality and environmental justice.

MEMPHIS, Tenn . — On Tuesday, the Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of the NAACP, sent a letter to xAI signaling their intent to sue over the company's continued use of unpermitted gas turbines at its data center in South Memphis. The letter explains how xAI, a company founded by Elon Musk, has violated federal law by installing dozens of polluting methane gas turbines at its data center without any of the required permits or best available pollution controls. The 60-day Notice of Intent to Sue is a prerequisite to filing a lawsuit under the Clean Air Act. "All too often, big corporations like xAI treat our communities and families like obstacles to be pushed aside," said NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson . "We cannot afford to normalize this kind of environmental injustice — where billion-dollar companies set up polluting operations in Black neighborhoods without any permits and think they'll get away with it because the people don't have the power to fight back. We will not allow xAI to get away with this." XAI began operations at its South Memphis data center in June of 2024. To meet the facility's massive power demands, the company began installing dozens of polluting methane gas turbines without any permits. Aerial images obtained by SELC revealed 35 turbines at the site in March, and follow-up thermal images obtained in April showed that nearly all of the turbines were emitting significant amounts of heat, indicating they were running. New satellite images show that, while the company has removed some smaller-sized turbines, it has recently installed three larger turbines. "XAI's decision to install and operate dozens of polluting gas turbines without any permits or public oversight is a clear violation of the Clean Air Act," SELC Senior Attorney Patrick Anderson said. "Over the last year, these turbines have pumped out pollution that threatens the health of Memphis families. This notice paves the way for a lawsuit that can hold xAI accountable for its unlawful refusal to get permits for its gas turbines." Gas turbines release smog-forming pollution and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde. These pollutants are tied to increases in asthma, respiratory diseases, heart problems, and certain cancers. XAI's South Memphis data center is located near predominantly Black communities that are already overburdened with industrial pollution from dozens of industrial facilities, including an oil refinery, a steel mill, and a TVA gas plant. Studies show that Boxtown, the neighborhood closest to the xAI data center, faces a cancer risk four times the national average. The Memphis metro area already struggles with significant and growing problems with ozone pollution — better known as smog. The last four years of air monitoring data show that the Memphis metro area is violating national smog standards and that the problem is getting worse, not better. This year, Shelby County once again received an "F" for ozone pollution from the American Lung Association . XAI has faced significant public pushback from Memphians over the last year. Community groups have held protests as hundreds of people submitted comments to the Shelby County Health Department in opposition to the company's use of polluting gas turbines. Community members have also raised serious questions about xAI's second South Memphis data center, located in the Whitehaven community. The company has not said how that facility would be powered, creating concerns that xAI could install more polluting gas turbines in the Memphis area. Local and federal regulations require xAI to obtain appropriate air permits before operating its polluting gas turbines. While some local leaders, including the Memphis Mayor and Shelby County Health Department, have claimed there is a "364-exemption" for xAI's gas turbines, they have never been able to point to a specific exemption that would apply to turbines as large as the ones at the xAI site. About NAACP The NAACP advocates, agitates, and litigates for the civil rights due to Black America. Our legacy is built on the foundation of grassroots activism by the biggest civil rights pioneers of the 20th century and is sustained by 21st century activists. From classrooms and courtrooms to city halls and Congress, our network of members across the country works to secure the social and political power that will end race-based discrimination. That work is rooted in racial equity, civic engagement, and supportive policies and institutions for all marginalized people. We are committed to a world without racism where Black people enjoy equitable opportunities in thriving communities. NOTE: The Legal Defense Fund – also referred to as the NAACP-LDF - was founded in 1940 as a part of the NAACP, but now operates as a completely separate entity. The Southern Environmental Law Center is one of the nation's most powerful defenders of the environment, rooted in the South. With a long track record, SELC takes on the toughest environmental challenges in court, in government, and in our communities to protect our region's air, water, climate, wildlife, lands, and people. Nonprofit and nonpartisan, the organization has a staff of 200, including more than 130 legal and policy experts, and is headquartered in Charlottesville, Va., with offices in Asheville, Atlanta, Birmingham, Chapel Hill, Charleston, Nashville, Richmond, and Washington, D.C. You can become a Champion for Change and receive a t-shirt with your monthly gift of $19 a month or more right now.

A federal judge in Mississippi has rejected an effort by the Trump administration to shut down a lawsuit brought by the NAACP against Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, allowing a closely watched environmental justice case to continue. The lawsuit, filed by the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of operating a gas-fired power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, without the environmental permits required under the Clean Air Act. The plant supplies power to xAI’s massive Colossus 2 data center, which supports the company’s artificial intelligence operations. The case has drawn attention because of the plant’s location near predominantly Black communities in North Mississippi and South Memphis. Reuters previously reported that pollution tied to the project has raised concerns about whether the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is placing disproportionate environmental burdens on Black neighborhoods. The Trump administration, acting through the Environmental Protection Agency, sought to intervene in the case and argued that the EPA had the authority to terminate the lawsuit. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown disagreed with that position Monday. Brown ruled that the EPA could participate in the case, but said nothing in the Clean Air Act gives the agency the power to unilaterally dismiss a citizen lawsuit simply because it has intervened. The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved. The lawsuit was originally filed in April. At the time, the NAACP accused xAI of operating dozens of methane gas turbines without the required permits, effectively creating a private power plant to meet the enormous energy demands of its data center. The organization has argued that nearby residents should not have to bear the health and environmental costs of the company’s rapid expansion. The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution. The organization is being represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice. The legal fight comes as communities across the country begin confronting the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, and developers are increasingly turning to on-site power generation to meet demand. That growth has prompted new questions about air quality, energy use and how quickly environmental regulations can keep pace with the AI boom. For the NAACP, the case is about more than one data center. It is part of a broader argument that Black communities should not be expected to absorb additional pollution in the name of technological progress, particularly when those communities have historically faced disproportionate exposure to industrial development and poor air quality. The judge’s ruling does not determine whether xAI violated environmental law. That question still has to be resolved in court. What it does mean is that the NAACP will be allowed to continue pressing its case.

extraction.body: A federal judge just handed the NAACP a major victory in its fight against xAI, allowing a lawsuit alleging Clean Air Act violations at the company's data center to move forward. With AI data centers consuming unprecedented amounts of energy and requiring extensive cooling systems, the ruling could reshape how tech companies approach regulatory compliance. The legal battle puts xAI, Elon Musk's artificial intelligence venture, squarely in the crosshairs of environmental justice advocates who argue the company's data center operations violate federal clean air standards. The judge's decision to let the case proceed past preliminary motions means xAI will now face discovery and potentially a trial on the merits of the NAACP's claims. Just last week, SpaceX closed a massive $40 billion debt deal to purchase GPUs for AI infrastructure, underscoring the breakneck pace of expansion across Musk's technology empire. That infrastructure buildout requires enormous data centers with corresponding energy demands and environmental footprints. The NAACP's lawsuit centers on allegations that xAI's data center operations produce air pollution that exceeds Clean Air Act thresholds without proper permitting or mitigation measures. Environmental advocates have increasingly raised concerns about the energy intensity of AI model training and inference, which requires thousands of high-powered chips running continuously in facilities that generate substantial heat and emissions. Data centers have become flashpoints in communities across the country as residents push back against facilities they see as bringing pollution, noise, and strain on local power grids without commensurate benefits. The judge's ruling doesn't determine the merits of the NAACP's claims, but it does mean the organization cleared the initial hurdles to proceed with litigation. That's significant because tech companies often succeed in getting environmental lawsuits dismissed on procedural grounds before reaching the substance of the allegations. For xAI, the lawsuit adds regulatory uncertainty at a crucial moment. The company competes with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta in the race to build more powerful AI systems, a competition that requires massive infrastructure investments. Companies have announced plans for dozens of new data centers to support AI workloads, often in regions offering tax incentives or cheap power. Legal experts say the case could establish important precedents about what level of environmental review and permitting AI data centers require. The Clean Air Act includes provisions for reviewing major new sources of pollution and protecting communities disproportionately affected by environmental hazards, both potentially relevant to large-scale AI infrastructure. The lawsuit also highlights tensions within Musk's broader business empire. The company's rapid growth has occasionally outpaced its ability to navigate complex regulatory frameworks. The case now moves into discovery, where the NAACP will have the opportunity to gather evidence about xAI's operations, emissions, and compliance with air quality standards. That process could reveal new details about how the company manages the environmental impacts of its data center operations and whether it obtained necessary permits before beginning operations. For the NAACP, the ruling represents validation of its strategy to use environmental law as a tool for protecting communities from the potential harms of AI infrastructure expansion. The organization has increasingly focused on technology policy issues, recognizing that decisions about where to locate data centers and other facilities have significant equity implications. The judge's decision to let this lawsuit proceed signals that AI companies can't assume their infrastructure expansion will face only technical and financial hurdles. As xAI and its rivals pour billions into data centers, they'll need to navigate not just the engineering challenges of training massive models, but also the regulatory and legal frameworks designed to protect air quality and environmental justice.

MEMPHIS, Tenn . — On Tuesday, the Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of the NAACP, sent a letter to xAI signaling their intent to sue over the company's continued use of unpermitted gas turbines at its data center in South Memphis. The letter explains how xAI, a company founded by Elon Musk, has violated federal law by installing dozens of polluting methane gas turbines at its data center without any of the required permits or best available pollution controls. The 60-day Notice of Intent to Sue is a prerequisite to filing a lawsuit under the Clean Air Act. "All too often, big corporations like xAI treat our communities and families like obstacles to be pushed aside," said NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson . "We cannot afford to normalize this kind of environmental injustice — where billion-dollar companies set up polluting operations in Black neighborhoods without any permits and think they'll get away with it because the people don't have the power to fight back. We will not allow xAI to get away with this." XAI began operations at its South Memphis data center in June of 2024. To meet the facility's massive power demands, the company began installing dozens of polluting methane gas turbines without any permits. Aerial images obtained by SELC revealed 35 turbines at the site in March, and follow-up thermal images obtained in April showed that nearly all of the turbines were emitting significant amounts of heat, indicating they were running. New satellite images show that, while the company has removed some smaller-sized turbines, it has recently installed three larger turbines. "XAI's decision to install and operate dozens of polluting gas turbines without any permits or public oversight is a clear violation of the Clean Air Act," SELC Senior Attorney Patrick Anderson said. "Over the last year, these turbines have pumped out pollution that threatens the health of Memphis families. This notice paves the way for a lawsuit that can hold xAI accountable for its unlawful refusal to get permits for its gas turbines." Gas turbines release smog-forming pollution and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde. These pollutants are tied to increases in asthma, respiratory diseases, heart problems, and certain cancers. XAI's South Memphis data center is located near predominantly Black communities that are already overburdened with industrial pollution from dozens of industrial facilities, including an oil refinery, a steel mill, and a TVA gas plant. Studies show that Boxtown, the neighborhood closest to the xAI data center, faces a cancer risk four times the national average. The Memphis metro area already struggles with significant and growing problems with ozone pollution — better known as smog. The last four years of air monitoring data show that the Memphis metro area is violating national smog standards and that the problem is getting worse, not better. This year, Shelby County once again received an "F" for ozone pollution from the American Lung Association . XAI has faced significant public pushback from Memphians over the last year. Community groups have held protests as hundreds of people submitted comments to the Shelby County Health Department in opposition to the company's use of polluting gas turbines. Community members have also raised serious questions about xAI's second South Memphis data center, located in the Whitehaven community. The company has not said how that facility would be powered, creating concerns that xAI could install more polluting gas turbines in the Memphis area. Local and federal regulations require xAI to obtain appropriate air permits before operating its polluting gas turbines. While some local leaders, including the Memphis Mayor and Shelby County Health Department, have claimed there is a "364-exemption" for xAI's gas turbines, they have never been able to point to a specific exemption that would apply to turbines as large as the ones at the xAI site. About NAACP The NAACP advocates, agitates, and litigates for the civil rights due to Black America. Our legacy is built on the foundation of grassroots activism by the biggest civil rights pioneers of the 20th century and is sustained by 21st century activists. From classrooms and courtrooms to city halls and Congress, our network of members across the country works to secure the social and political power that will end race-based discrimination. That work is rooted in racial equity, civic engagement, and supportive policies and institutions for all marginalized people. We are committed to a world without racism where Black people enjoy equitable opportunities in thriving communities. NOTE: The Legal Defense Fund – also referred to as the NAACP-LDF - was founded in 1940 as a part of the NAACP, but now operates as a completely separate entity. The Southern Environmental Law Center is one of the nation's most powerful defenders of the environment, rooted in the South. With a long track record, SELC takes on the toughest environmental challenges in court, in government, and in our communities to protect our region's air, water, climate, wildlife, lands, and people. Nonprofit and nonpartisan, the organization has a staff of 200, including more than 130 legal and policy experts, and is headquartered in Charlottesville, Va., with offices in Asheville, Atlanta, Birmingham, Chapel Hill, Charleston, Nashville, Richmond, and Washington, D.C. MEMPHIS, Tenn . — On Tuesday, the Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of the NAACP, sent a letter to xAI signaling their intent to sue over the company's continued use of unpermitted gas turbines at its data center in South Memphis.

The letter explains how xAI, a company founded by Elon Musk, has violated federal law by installing dozens of polluting methane gas turbines at its data center without any of the required permits or best available pollution controls. The 60-day Notice of Intent to Sue is a prerequisite to filing a lawsuit under the Clean Air Act.

"All too often, big corporations like xAI treat our communities and families like obstacles to be pushed aside," said NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson . "We cannot afford to normalize this kind of environmental injustice — where billion-dollar companies set up polluting operations in Black neighborhoods without any permits and think they'll get away with it because the people don't have the power to fight back. We will not allow xAI to get away with this."

XAI began operations at its South Memphis data center in June of 2024. To meet the facility's massive power demands, the company began installing dozens of polluting methane gas turbines without any permits. Aerial images obtained by SELC revealed 35 turbines at the site in March, and follow-up thermal images obtained in April showed that nearly all of the turbines were emitting significant amounts of heat, indicating they were running. New satellite images show that, while the company has removed some smaller-sized turbines, it has recently installed three larger turbines.

"XAI's decision to install and operate dozens of polluting gas turbines without any permits or public oversight is a clear violation of the Clean Air Act," SELC Senior Attorney Patrick Anderson said. "Over the last year, these turbines have pumped out pollution that threatens the health of Memphis families. This notice paves the way for a lawsuit that can hold xAI accountable for its unlawful refusal to get permits for its gas turbines."

Gas turbines release smog-forming pollution and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde. These pollutants are tied to increases in asthma, respiratory diseases, heart problems, and certain cancers. XAI's South Memphis data center is located near predominantly Black communities that are already overburdened with industrial pollution from dozens of industrial facilities, including an oil refinery, a steel mill, and a TVA gas plant. Studies show that Boxtown, the neighborhood closest to the xAI data center, faces a cancer risk four times the national average.

The Memphis metro area already struggles with significant and growing problems with ozone pollution — better known as smog. The last four years of air monitoring data show that the Memphis metro area is violating national smog standards and that the problem is getting worse, not better. This year, Shelby County once again received an "F" for ozone pollution from the American Lung Association .

XAI has faced significant public pushback from Memphians over the last year. Community groups have held protests as hundreds of people submitted comments to the Shelby County Health Department in opposition to the company's use of polluting gas turbines.

Community members have also raised serious questions about xAI's second South Memphis data center, located in the Whitehaven community. The company has not said how that facility would be powered, creating concerns that xAI could install more polluting gas turbines in the Memphis area.

Local and federal regulations require xAI to obtain appropriate air permits before operating its polluting gas turbines. While some local leaders, including the Memphis Mayor and Shelby County Health Department, have claimed there is a "364-exemption" for xAI's gas turbines, they have never been able to point to a specific exemption that would apply to turbines as large as the ones at the xAI site.
